units.la: QVAESTIONES MISCELLAE ex Physica. QUAESTIO I.
units.tr: Miscellaneous Questions on Physics. Question I.

units.la: Quodnam sit objectum per se, adaequatum & legitimum Physica?
units.tr: What is the proper, adequate and legitimate object of Physics?

units.la: Vid verba quaeris? Veritas odit moras, Romanę sapientiae scitum est; quare ἄτερ πεϱοιμιῶν ad rem. Ad enodandam hanc thesin sequentia praenotamus. I. Objectum per se, adaequatum alicujus disciplinae, quod aliter vocatur objectum per se totale, & objectum per se primo, seu primarium, esse illud, quod terminat omnes actus proprios alicujus disciplinae, & ad quod referuntur omnia, quae tractantur in illa, vel tanquam principia & causae, vel tanquam proprietates, vel tanquam species.
units.tr: Do you ask for words? Truth hates delay, as the Roman saying goes, so let us come to the matter without preamble [ἄτερ προοιμίων]. To explain this thesis, we first set out the following. I. The proper and adequate object of any discipline, which is also called the total proper object or the primary proper object, is that which terminates all the proper acts of the discipline and to which everything treated in it is referred, either as principles and causes, or as properties, or as species.

units.la: Dicimus II. Tale objectum esse considerandum, vel quoad formale, vel quoad materiale. Materiale nihil aliud est, quàm res considerata, quae tractatur in disciplina; Formale est ipse modus considerandi. Cùm enim materiale alicujus disciplinae possit esse commune cum aliis disciplinis, per modum illum considerandi, quem quaevis disciplina habet proprium, res consideranda, seu objectum illud materiale, ad hanc vel illam disciplinam determinatur, & fit alicujus disciplinae proprium, sub illa ratione formali, sub qua illa objectum suum contemplatur.
units.tr: We say II. that such an object must be considered either with respect to its formal aspect or its material aspect. The material aspect is nothing other than the thing considered and treated in the discipline. The formal aspect is the very mode of considering it. For although the material of a discipline may be common to other disciplines, the thing to be considered, or that material object, is determined to this or that discipline by the mode of considering it proper to each discipline, and so becomes the proper possession of that discipline under the formal aspect under which it contemplates its object.

units.la: Dicimus III. Varios esse authores in assignando Physicae objecto: omnem autem varietatem inter eos esse potius de voce, quàm verò de re ipsa, cùm quo ad rem ipsam omnino conveniant, & solùm quantum ad modum explicandi, & dicendi differentiant: Alii enim objectum legitimum Physicae volunt Ens naturale, alii substantiam naturalem, alii Ens mobile, alii corpus mobile, quorum sententiam prolixiori tractu orationis persequitur Zabarella de Natu-ralis scientiae constitutione lib. I. cap. aliquot p. 3.4. & sequentibus. Benedictus Pererius lib. II. de Philosophia naturali cap. I. p. 61. & seq. De Raconis praeludiis Physicis sectione II. p. 29. fatentur enim omnes objectum illud esse id, quod vocamus corpus naturale, id est, quod in se habet principium motus & quietis, seu materiam & formam.
units.tr: We say III. that authors vary in assigning the object of Physics, but that all the variation among them concerns the word rather than the thing itself. For they agree entirely about the thing and differ only in the manner of explaining and stating it. Some want the legitimate object of Physics to be natural being, others natural substance, others mobile being, others mobile body. Zabarella pursues their opinions at greater length in his De naturalis scientiae constitutione, book I, chapter several, pages 3 and 4 and following. See also Benedictus Pererius, De philosophia naturali, book II, chapter I, page 61 and following; and De Raconis, Praeludia physica, section II, page 29. For all of them admit that the object is that which we call natural body, that is, what has within itself the principle of motion and rest, that is, matter and form.

units.la: His praenotatis respondemus; objectum per se, adaequatum, & legitimum PhyPhysicæ, conplectens sub se materiale & formale, esse corpus naturale, quâ naturale Cùm nempe in Physica, omnia quæ in illa tractantur, vel tanquam principia, & causæ, vel tanquam proprietates, vel tanquam species referantur ad corpus naturale, utique illud objectum per se adæquatum Physicæ nemo negabit.
units.tr: With these preliminaries, we answer: the proper, adequate and legitimate object of Physics, comprehending under itself both the material and the formal aspect, is natural body, insofar as it is natural. Since in Physics all the things treated in it, whether as principles and causes, or as properties, or as species, are referred to natural body, no one will deny that this is the object proper and adequate to Physics.

units.la: Confirmatur hæc nostra assertio ex eo, quòd hæc attributa, causæ, & proprietates, quæ in nulla alia disciplina, quàm in Physica, de subjecto demonstrantur, nulli alii rei tribui possunt per se, quàm corpori naturali, cùm enti tantùm conveniat per accidens, esse naturale, seu constare materia & forma, quatenus Ens per materiam & formam ad corpus naturale restringitur. Materia enim Physica seu sensibilis, & forma, quæ constituit naturam, & natura, quæ sola est principium intrinsecum motus & quietis, soli corpori competit; ac consequenter naturale, quod est formale seu ratio formalis objecti Physicæ, cùm soli corpori competit, utique solum corpus naturale adæquatum Physicæ subjectum seu objectum esse potest.
units.tr: This assertion of ours is confirmed by the fact that these attributes, causes and properties, which are demonstrated of their subject in no discipline other than Physics, can be ascribed through themselves to no thing other than natural body. Being can have being natural, that is, consist of matter and form, only accidentally, insofar as Being is restricted to natural body through matter and form. For physical or sensible matter, and the form which constitutes nature, and nature itself, which alone is the intrinsic principle of motion and rest, belong to body alone. Consequently, the natural, which is the formal aspect or formal notion of the object of Physics, belongs to body alone, and so only natural body can be the adequate subject or object of Physics.

units.la: Theophilus Territius, in Philosophia sua Christiana, pag 95.96.97.98.&c. Hoc objectum Physicæ dicit esse inadæquatum: quia illud sit objectum adæquatum Physicæ, cui primò, & per se, & reciprocè conveniant proprietates primariæ, quæ demonstrantur in Physica, scilicet mobilitas & quiescibilitas intrinseca & sensibilis, at verò has proprietates reciprocari tantùm cum Ente naturali, non autem cum substantia, & corpore naturali: licet nempe omne corpus naturale sit intrinsecè mobile & quiescibile, non tamen quicquid est intrinsecè mobile & quiescibile esse corpus naturale; cùm qualitates Physicæ, ut calor, frigus, & aliæ, sint vera accidentia, & sint intrinsecè mobiles & quiescibiles; Cùm actionem imprimant potentiæ sensitivæ.
units.tr: Theophilus Territius, in his Philosophia Christiana, pages 95, 96, 97, 98 and following, says that this object of Physics is inadequate. For the adequate object of Physics, he says, is that to which the primary properties demonstrated in Physics belong first, through itself, and reciprocally, namely intrinsic and sensible mobility and quiescibility. But these properties, he argues, are reciprocated only with natural being and not with natural substance or natural body. For although every natural body is intrinsically mobile and quiescible, not everything that is intrinsically mobile and quiescible is a natural body. Physical qualities such as heat, cold and others are true accidents, and they are intrinsically mobile and quiescible, since they impress their action on the sensitive powers.

units.la: Verùm respondeo 1. Objecto alicujus disciplinæ immediatè debere convenire proprietates, quæ explicantur in illa scientia, at proprietates objecti Physicæ non conveniunt immediatè Enti; quia Enti non conveniunt sub ratione Entis, sed tantùm sub ratione corporis, ut supra: Confirmatur: Si nempe illæ proprietates objecti Physicæ, causæ & principia, convenirent Enti, quà Ens est, tum omne Ens esset mobile, quantum, materiatum, &c. At hoc absurdum; quærendum igitur est proprium aliud subjectum, cui per se & primò infit natura, & principium motus & quietis, & propter quod etiam competat aliis rebus, v.gr. in tabula substantiæ, quæ est ex Petro, Homine, Animali, vivente, corpore, substantia, & Ente, illud quod est infra corpus non proprie respondet v.gr. mobili, quoniam est angustius & minùs latè patens, cùm pluribus rebus competat mobilitas, quàm viventi, Animali, Homini, Petro, quæ tamen sub corpore in hac serie comprehenduntur: Illa autem quæ sunt supra corpus, latius patent quàm mobile, cùm non omne Ens sit mobile, in ratione Entis: ex quibus intelligitur, esse mobile, non esse conjungendum reciprocabiliter, cum illis, quæ sunt supra corpus, sicque non rectè statui objectum Physicæ Ens naturale, seu mobile. Respondeo II. In probatione argumenti, committi fallaciam à non causa ut causa; Dicimus enim subjectum Physicæ esse corpus naturale, id est, quod habet principium motus & quietis, id est, materiam & formam, at verò accidentia illa, non habent materiam, & formam adeoque nec principium motus & quietis, sic non sunt mobilia, neque quiescibilia. Ad hæc objectum Physicæ, si debeat esse mobile, tum illæ qualitates, etiamsi actionem imprimant potentiæ sensitivæ, nec ita objectum Physicæ adæquatum, & objectum Demonstrationis esse possunt, cùm objectum ejus non debeat esse movens, sed mobile; Res enim aliqua non est naturalis, quia movet, sed quia naturaliter movetur, cùm natura definiatur esse causa, ut id, in quo inest, moveatur, & quiescat. Vide de hac materia Pererium libr. II. de Philosophia Naturali p. 73. 75. Derodonem Phys. proœmio, artic. IV. Stierium proœmio Physicæ quæst. II. p. 2. plures alios.
units.tr: But I answer, first, that properties explained in a science must belong immediately to the object of that science. The properties of the object of Physics do not belong immediately to being, because they do not belong to being under the aspect of being but only under the aspect of body, as above. This is confirmed: if those properties of the object of Physics, causes and principles, belonged to being insofar as it is being, then every being would be mobile, quantified, material, and so on. But this is absurd. We must therefore seek another proper subject to which nature and the principle of motion and rest belong first and through itself, and on account of which it also belongs to other things. For example, in the table of substance, which runs from Peter, to Man, Animal, living thing, body, substance, and Being, the item that is below body does not properly correspond to, say, mobile, since it is narrower and extends less widely, because mobility belongs to more things than living, animal, man or Peter, which nevertheless are included under body in this series. Those items that are above body extend more widely than mobile, since not every being is mobile in the notion of being. From this it is understood that mobile is not to be reciprocally conjoined with those things that are above body, and so it is not rightly established that the object of Physics is natural being, or mobile being. Second, I answer that in the proof of the argument there is a fallacy of treating a non-cause as a cause. For we say that the subject of Physics is natural body, that is, what has the principle of motion and rest, that is, matter and form. But those accidents do not have matter and form, and therefore do not have the principle of motion and rest; thus they are neither mobile nor quiescible. Moreover, if the object of Physics must be mobile, then those qualities, even if they impress their action on the sensitive powers, cannot be the adequate object of Physics and the object of demonstration, since its object ought to be what is moved, not what moves. For a thing is not natural because it moves, but because it is moved naturally, since nature is defined as the cause by which that in which it inheres is moved and at rest. See on this matter Pererius, De philosophia naturali, book II, pages 73 and 75; Derodon, Physica, preface, article IV; Stierius, preface to Physica, question II, page 2; and many others.

units.la: QUÆSTIO II.
units.tr: QUESTION II.

units.la: An materia prima habeat proprium actum Entitativum?
units.tr: Whether prime matter has its own entitative act?

units.la: Si quæ in Philosophia opinio difficultatibus inextricabilibus ferè est involuta, ea est, quæ ceu ἐχίδνα pomum, de prima rerum materia in scholarum pulvere, non exiguos hactenus dedit motus, ut Conimbricenses ignorando eam cognosci, & cognoscendo ignorari libere fateantur; Ut ita, quid illa propriè sit, difficillimû hactenus dictu fuerit, explicatuq;. Hinc tot litigia de ejus existentia; an scil. existentiam ex sese habeat, an verò per formam? Negativæ quidem suos calculos addiderunt Thomas 1. part. q. 44. art. 2. ad 3. Conimbricenses actum omnem, etiam entitativum materiæ negant l. I cap. IX. q. 3. Articulo I. p. 198. 199. Quibus sese agglomerat Zabarel l. 2. de prima rerum materia capitibus aliquot, p. 177. & seq. Eis tamen sese opposuerunt; Scotus, & qui sub ejus nomine militant. Toletus lib. I. cap. 7. p. mihi 34. Pererius lib. V. cap 13. p. m. 310. Quidam sententiam suam ex aliorum judiciis suspendunt, & cùm in re à Scoto non dissideant, modum tamen loquendi non probant; fatentur enim illi, materiam habere propriam, existentiam distinctā ab existentia formæ, & consequenter docent materiam actu esse extra nihilum existentiæ; negant tamen dicendum esse actum entitativum, ob leviusculas rationes aliquas. Quorum tamen judicium Suarezius aliqualiter tolerandum putat, cùm in re à veritatis tramite non deviant, sed tantùm in modo loquendi. Vide Suarezium Disp. Metaph. XIII. pag. 286. & seq.
units.tr: If there is any opinion in philosophy that is nearly inextricably tangled in difficulties, it is the one about prime matter of things, which, like an apple of Echidna [ἐχίδνα], has stirred up no small disputes in the dust of the schools. The Conimbricenses freely confess that it is known by not being known and is not known by being known, so that what it properly is has hitherto been very hard to say or explain. Hence so many disputes about its existence: does it have existence from itself, or only through its form? Those who deny it have added their own calculations: Thomas, in the first part, question 44, article 2, reply to objection 3; the Conimbricenses, in book I, chapter IX, question 3, article 1, pages 198 and 199, deny that matter has any act at all, even an entitative one. Zabarella joins them in several chapters of his second book on prime matter, pages 177 and following. Nevertheless, Scotus and those who fight under his name have opposed them, as have Toletus, book I, chapter 7, page 34 of my edition, and Pererius, book V, chapter 13, page 310 of my edition. Some suspend their judgment on the opinion of others: although they do not disagree with Scotus on the matter itself, they do not approve his way of speaking. For they admit that matter has its own existence, distinct from the existence of the form, and consequently they teach that matter is actually outside nothing in existence; yet they deny that it should be called an entitative act, on account of some rather slight reasons. Suarez thinks that their judgment is to be tolerated to some extent, since they do not stray from the path of truth in the thing itself, but only in the way of speaking. See Suarez, Metaphysical Disputations XIII, pages 286 and following.

units.la: In antecessum præsupponimus. I. Per existentiam nihil aliud intelligi, quàm actum entitativum, seu existentem, & sic omne id, quod verè existit, esse in actu entitativo; illud autem verè existere, juxta plerorumque sententiam, quod est extra causas suas. Quando nempe est adhuc in potentia ad fieri, seu produci, vocatur potentia objectiva, seu objectum potentiæ productivæ, cùm verò jam productum, & extra causas constitutum est, habet actum entitativum, seu actum existentem, qui illi potentiæ objectivæ respondet, competitque omni enti, quod est in rerum natura.
units.tr: We presuppose the following. I. By existence we understand nothing other than entitative act, or actual existing; so everything that truly exists is in entitative act. According to the view of most, a thing truly exists when it is outside its causes. When it is still in potency to come to be, or to be produced, it is called objective potency, or the object of a productive potency. When it has been produced and set up outside its causes, it has entitative act, or existing act, which corresponds to that objective potency and belongs to every being that is in the nature of things.

units.la: Dicimus II. Potentiam dici ex relatione ad actum, & actum ex relatione ad potentiam: idem ergo esse quærere, utrum materia sit pura potentia Metaphysica, ac quærere, utrum nullum actum Metaphysicum includat.
units.tr: We say II. that potency is spoken of in relation to act, and act in relation to potency. So to ask whether matter is pure metaphysical potency is the same as asking whether it includes no metaphysical act.

units.la: His præsuppositis cum tota Scotistarum turba dicimus, materiam non esse puram potentiam in genere entis, seu actus Metaphysici, sed habere actum suum entitativum à se ipsa, non à forma substantiali, esse verò in potentia ad actum formalem, ad quem est in potentia subjectiva, id quod sic probamus.
units.tr: With these presuppositions, we say with the whole crowd of Scotists that matter is not pure potency in the genus of being, or metaphysical act. Rather, it has its own entitative act from itself, not from substantial form, while it is in potency to formal act, to which it stands in subjective potency. We prove this as follows.

units.la: I. Quod dependet ab alio in esse & in conservari, illud ei, à quo dependet non dat existentiam. Sed formæ omnes, excepta anima rationali, dependent in esse & in conservari à materia: E. forma materiæ non dat existentiam. Major certa est, cùm conformius sit naturis rerum, ut subjecta & illa, à quibus res dependent, & in quibus subjectantur, dependentibus dent existentiam, quàm vicissim. Adde quòd potius sequatur, subjecta habere propriam existentiam, cùm ordine naturæ ea antecedant, quæ ab ipsis dependent; & hoc ex ratione subjecti facile colligitur, nam in primo subjecto, necessaria est realis potentia passiva, vel potius ipsummet essentialiter est potentia passiva; non potest autem intelligi potentia passiva realis, sine aliqua actualitate entitativa. Qualiter enim potest intelligi, quòd aliquid sit verè & realiter receptivum alterius, nisi in se aliquid sit. Hinc ipse Thomas 1.parte, quæst.46.artic.ait: Materiam non dici esse in potentia, eo modo, quo dicitur esse in potentia Ens posisibile, ex sola non repugnantia terminorum; supponit ergo esse aliquod Ens actu fundans realem potentiam passivam, vel quòd potius sit realis potentia passiva in genere substantiæ. Minor quoque facile probatur ex eo, quòd formæ omnes, exceptâ animâ rationali, sint materiales, seu tales, quæ in fieri, & esse à materia dependeant, & in hoc ipso contradistinguantur animæ rationali, immateriali formæ, quæ ut est à materia separabilis, ita propriam habet subsistentiam.
units.tr: I. What depends on another for its being and for its preservation does not give existence to that on which it depends. But all forms, except the rational soul, depend on matter for their being and preservation. Therefore the form of matter does not give existence. The major premise is certain, since it is more in keeping with the natures of things that subjects, and those things on which dependent things rest and in which they inhere, should give existence to dependent things, than the reverse. Add that it follows rather that subjects have their own existence, since in the order of nature they precede those things which depend on them. This is easily gathered from the notion of a subject: in the first subject a real passive potency is necessary, or rather it is itself essentially passive potency; but real passive potency cannot be understood without some entitative actuality. For how can something be understood to be truly and really receptive of another, unless it is something in itself? Hence Thomas himself, in the first part, q. 46, art., says that matter is not said to be in potency in the way that a possible being is said to be in potency, from the mere non-repugnance of terms. He therefore supposes that there is some being actually grounding a real passive potency, or rather that matter is real passive potency in the genus of substance. The minor premise is also easily proved from the fact that all forms, except the rational soul, are material, that is, such as depend on matter in becoming and in being. In this very respect they are distinguished from the rational soul, an immaterial form, which, since it is separable from matter, has its own subsistence.

units.la: II. Si forma materiæ daret existentiam, tunc toties materia produceretur de novo, & corrumperetur, sicque mutaret existentiam, quoties novam formam acquirit; quod necessariò dicendum à Thomistis, quia existentia materiæ, fiesset propria formæ, toties deberet mutari, quoties ipsa forma. Sed falsum & absurdum consequens, E. & antecedens. Consequentiam probo; quia rem aliquam produci, est eam accipere existentiam. E. Si per formam actu informantem, habet materia suam existentiam, sequitur quoties materia unam formam amittit, & aliam recipit, toties eam corrumpi, atq; ita desinere esse, in rerum natura, & de novo produci, sicque esse corruptibilem & non esse perpetuam. Antecedens probo; quia rem produci, est eam extra suas causas constitui, & eam corrumpi est desinere esse extra suas causas; E. Rem produci est eam accipere existentiam, & corrumpi, est eam amittere existentiam. Ratio consequentiæ, quia existentia est id, per quod res creata est formaliter extra suas causas.
units.tr: II. If the form of matter gave existence, then matter would be produced anew and corrupted, and so would change its existence, as often as it acquires a new form. The Thomists must necessarily say this, because the existence of matter would belong to the form, and would have to change as often as the form itself does. But the consequent is false and absurd, and therefore so is the antecedent. I prove the consequence: to be produced is to receive existence. So if matter has its existence through the form actually informing it, it follows that as often as matter loses one form and receives another, so often it is corrupted, ceases to be in the nature of things, and is produced anew; and so it is corruptible and not perpetual. I prove the antecedent: to be produced is to be set up outside one's causes, and to be corrupted is to cease to be outside one's causes. Therefore to be produced is to receive existence, and to be corrupted is to lose existence. The reason for the consequence is that existence is that through which a created thing is formally outside its causes.

units.la: Minor argumenti principalis probatur: quia ab Aristotelicis ipsis conceditur, à plerisque etiam melioris notæ Philosophis, materiam primam esse ingenerabilem & incorruptibilem, corruptibilitate scilicet Physica, eo quòd à nulla causa naturali in fieri dependeat, ac proinde nec inconservari, quæ intelligenda in esse reduplicativo. Adde quòd materia prima si sit corruptibilis corruptione Physica, debeat corrumpi per solam resolutionem, adeoque resolvi in aliam priorem materiam: sed hoc absurdum; sic nempe materia prima non foret prima, sicque fieret progressus in infinitum. Sed debet annihilari; at verò nihil potest annihilari, seu in nihilum positionis, seu existentiæ redigi à causa aliqua naturali, sed sola supernaturali, ac proinde corruptione Metaphysica. Concedimus materiæ primæ corruptibilitatem subjectivam, objectivam denegamus.
units.tr: The minor premise of the main argument is proved as follows: even the Aristotelians themselves concede, and most philosophers of better repute as well, that prime matter is ungenerable and incorruptible, with physical incorruptibility, namely because it depends on no natural cause in its coming to be, and therefore not in its preservation either, which is to be understood in the reduplicative sense of being. Add that if prime matter were corruptible with physical corruption, it would have to be corrupted by mere resolution, and so be resolved into another, prior matter. But this is absurd: prime matter would then not be first, and an infinite regress would result. Rather, it must be annihilated; yet nothing can be annihilated, that is, reduced to nothing in its position or existence, by any natural cause, but only by a supernatural one, and therefore by metaphysical corruption. We concede to prime matter a subjective corruptibility; the objective kind we deny.

units.la: III. Materia egressa ex potentia objectiva accipit illico actum, qui absorbeat istam potentiam, estque ille actus existentiæ. At hic actus non convenit ei per formam, quia materia in ordine ad formam, est adhuc in pura potentia passiva. E. hunc actum materia habebit à se ipsa: A se ipsa, non removendo efficiens, sed removendo id, unde intrinsecè existat materia.
units.tr: III. Matter emerging from objective potency at once receives an act that absorbs that potency, and this act is the act of existence. But this act does not belong to matter through form, because in relation to form matter is still in pure passive potency. Therefore matter will have this act from itself: from itself not by removing the efficient cause, but by removing that from which matter would exist intrinsically.

units.la: Confirmatur hoc argumentum ex duplici consideratione seu habentia materiæ primæ, ante & post creationem; I. Consideratur ante creationem rerum, & sic ei nullus competit actus, nec formalis, nec entitativus, quia hoc modo in potentia objectiva est, cui opponitur actus entitativus. II. Consideratur post creationem, & sic tribuitur ei actus entitativus; ppost creationem, cùm existit, & definit esse in potentia objectiva, illi competit actus entitativus, siquidem actus entitativus complet potentiam objectivam, & hoc ipsum est, per quod definit esse in potentia objectiva.
units.tr: This argument is confirmed by a twofold consideration of prime matter, before and after creation. (I) Considered before the creation of things, it has no actuality at all, neither formal nor entitative, since in this state it is in objective potency, to which entitative actuality is opposed. (II) Considered after creation, it is ascribed entitative actuality: after creation, when it exists and ceases to be in objective potency, it possesses entitative actuality, since entitative actuality completes objective potency, and this very thing is that through which it ceases to be in objective potency.

units.la: Objicit Zabarella lib.II.de prima rerum materia cap II.p.182. Materiam non esse creatam tanquam rem quandam per se, & seorsim existentem, sed dicit potius esse concreatam, id est, creatam cum composito, & sub forma. Ex quo colligit nunquam fuisse impotentia objectiva seu objectum potentiæ creativæ.
units.tr: Zabarella objects, in book II, chapter II, page 182, of his work on prime matter, that matter was not created as a thing by itself and separately existing, but rather rightly said to be concreated, that is, created together with the composite and under a form. From this he concludes that it was never in objective potency, or the object of creative power.

units.la: Verùm respondeo I. Objectionem Zabarellæ petere τὸ ἀρχή; quia materia prima non potuit aliter fieri, quàm per creationem, eò ipso, quòd facta fit ex nihilo sui & subjecti: cum nempe sit materia prima, seu primum subjectum, non potest ex subjecto produci, supponeret namq; aliud subjectum, quod absurdum.
units.tr: But I reply, first, that Zabarella's objection begs the question (τὸ ἀρχή). For prime matter could not have been made otherwise than by creation, precisely because it is made out of nothing of its own and of a subject: since it is prime matter, that is, the first subject, it cannot be produced from a subject, for that would presuppose another subject, which is absurd.

units.la: Respondeo II. Licet materia non per se, & seorsim, sed sub forma & composito sit creata, sequitur tamen esse creatam, non quidem ut terminum creationis totalem & completum, sed ut partialem & incompletum. Atque hinc negari non potest, eam fuisse in potentia objectiva (nam esse in potentia objectiva, nihil aliud importat, quàm aliquid non esse, posse tamen esse, & fieri) quia jam est, & producta est, si non ut terminus productionis totalis, tamen ut partialis & incompletus.
units.tr: I reply, second, that although matter was created not by itself and separately, but under a form and in a composite, it does follow that it was created, not indeed as the whole and complete term of creation, but as a partial and incomplete term. And from this it cannot be denied that it was in objective potency (for to be in objective potency means nothing other than that a thing is not, yet is able to be and to become), because it now is, and has been produced, if not as the whole term of production, yet as a partial and incomplete one.

units.la: Multum praesidii sibi quaerunt adversarii in distinctione reali essentiae & existentiae, quam tamen nos pernegamus. Vide theses Derodonis de universali in communi p.52. Myllerum Metaph p.17. Burgersd.Metaph.p.55.plures alios. Nos paucis ita dicimus: Antequam res essent factae erant in se revera nihil, erant enim in potentia objectiva sed Ens in potentia objectiva, quatenus est in potentia objectiva ita distinguitur ab eo, quod actu est, ut nihil ab Ente distinguitur; Quando ergo creatura fit à Deo, existentia non additur essentiae, sed utraque simul producitur, sola enim ratione differunt. Si objicias, essentiam iis rebus tribui, quae adhuc sunt in potentia objectiva, atque adeo entia ea dici, saltem quatenus vox illa sumitur nominaliter, imò eodem modo entia dici, quo ea, quae jam existunt, ac proinde non esse nihil. Respondebo: negare me consequentiam; nam cum Ens dicitur de iis, quae non existunt actu, propositio vera est in sensu hypothetico, nihilque aliud significat, quàm ista entia fore, cum existent, similique modo essentia iis ex hypothesi tribuitur: Concedo etiam, non posse dici nihil purum, sed tantùm nihil essentiae, seu existentiae.
units.tr: Our adversaries seek much support in a real distinction between essence and existence, which we nonetheless flatly deny. See the theses of Derodon, On the Universal in General, page 52; Myller, Metaphysics, page 17; Burgersdijk, Metaphysics, page 55; and several others. We put it briefly as follows: before things were made they were in truth nothing in themselves, for they were in objective potency; but being in objective potency, insofar as it is in objective potency, is so distinguished from what is actually existing as nothing is distinguished from being. When therefore a creature is made by God, existence is not added to essence, but both are produced together, for they differ only in concept. If you object that essence is attributed to those things which are still in objective potency, and so they are called beings, at least insofar as that word is taken nominally, indeed in the same way as those things which now exist are called beings, and therefore are not nothing: I reply that I deny the consequence. For when Being is said of those things which do not actually exist, the proposition is true in a hypothetical sense, and signifies nothing other than that these beings will be when they exist; and in the same way essence is attributed to them on the hypothesis. I also concede that they cannot be called pure nothing, but only the nothing of essence or of existence.

units.la: Non jam metuimus argumentum Thomistarum, in quo tanquam in nodo Gordio mirè triumphant: Materiam primam esse Ens purâ potentiâ. Respondemus namque, non simpliciter esse intelligendum, sed tantùm respectu potentiae receptivae, quia est pura potentia receptiva, nullum includens de se actum formalem: quod optimè declaratur exemplo materiae rerum artificialium. Lignum v.gr. in se est actu corpus naturale: sed respectu formarum intraducendarum, est in mera potentia, quia ex se nullam habet actu, licèt eas possit recipere. Et haec quidem hactenus.
units.tr: We do not now fear the argument of the Thomists, in which they triumph as if over the Gordian knot: that prime matter is being of pure potency. For we reply that this must not be understood simply, but only with respect to receptive potency, since it is pure receptive potency, including in itself no formal actuality; which is very well illustrated by the example of the matter of artificial things. Wood, for instance, is in itself actually a natural body, but with respect to the forms to be introduced it is in mere potency, because from itself it has no actuality of them, although it can receive them. And so much for these matters.

units.la: QUAESTIO III.
units.tr: QUESTION III.

units.la: An unum numero corpus possit esse simul in pluribus locis, & plura numero corpora in unico loco?
units.tr: Can one body, numerically one, be in several places at once, and several bodies, numerically many, be in a single place?

units.la: Si quid unquam fuit, quod vel ipsum potuisset ad risum movere Heraclitum, hoc ipsum non immerito censetur, quo viri, acuti caeteroquin judicii, non-nun. nunquam cum bono dormitare videntur Homero, ut pudeat, hodieque hanc controversiam sub συζητήσεως vocare incudem, vel hoc ipso nomine, quòd ipsos quaestionis hujus authores, illius nondum pudeat, quâ tamen ita adhuc-dum cæcis judiciis delirant, ut malint perversas suas de theologia' sacra opiniones asserturi, ipsa naturæ, & philosophiæ sanioris succutere fundamenta, quàm veritati herbam porrigere. Nos totam controversiam paucis 'ita damus.: Vnum numero corpus virtute naturali non posse esse simul in pluribus locis, adæquatis omnes unanimi consensu largiuntur. An verò id super naturaliter fieri possit, acerrimè in Scholis disputatur. Affirmativa quidem vindices habet Pontificios, idoli panificii propugnatores, existimantes unum numero corpus posse simul esse in pluribus locis adæquatis supernaturaliter, seu virtute Divina: Quam quidem sententiam, duobus superstruunt fundamentis, tam egregnia, si DIs placet, nugatione dignis. 1. Quòd talis existentia unius corporis in pluribus locis non involvat contradictionem. 2. Quòd corpus Christi, sit in pluribus hostiis consecratis, atque adeò in pluribus locis; quibus quid stolidius confingi posit, ipso conjectore Oedippo vix videmus.
units.tr: If anything has ever been capable of moving Heraclitus to laughter, it is this controversy, which is rightly judged to be so, in which men otherwise of sharp judgment sometimes seem to nod off, as Homer did, to our shame. Even today they call this dispute an anvil of disputation [συζητήσεως], and the very name is apt, since the authors of this question are not yet ashamed of the question itself. Yet they rave with such blind judgments that they would rather, in defending their perverse opinions about sacred theology, shake the very foundations of nature and of sounder philosophy than yield the palm to truth. We grant the whole controversy in a few words: that one body, numerically one, cannot by natural power be at several places at once is conceded by all sides with one voice. But whether this can happen supernaturally is hotly debated in the schools. The affirmative has as its champions the Papists, the defenders of the bread-idol, who hold that one body, numerically one, can be at several places at once supernaturally, that is, by divine power. They build this opinion on two foundations, so trivial, God willing, that they deserve only mockery: (1) that such existence of one body in several places involves no contradiction; (2) that the body of Christ is in several consecrated hosts, and so in several places. One can hardly see what more foolish thing could be invented, even by Oedipus the riddle-solver himself.

units.la: Nos cum omnibus Orthodoxis utrumque negamus, etiam supernaturaliter, idque non ex defectu Dei, sed ex defectu rei, quia scilicet ipsam unius corporis naturam, & corporalem præsentiam penitùs subvertit. Et primò quidem, contra unius numero corporis πολυτοπίαν ita militamus. Quicquid involvit contradictionem, id ne quidem supernaturaliter esse potest. Sed idem numero corpus, esse simul in pluribus locis involvit contradictionem. Ergò idem numero corpus esse in pluribus locis simul, ne quidem supernaturaliter esse potest. Ratio majoris patet: quia illud, quod involvit contradictionem, seu prædicata contradictoria, est impossibile absolutè, sine habitudine ad aliquam potentiam, ob repugnantiam terminorum, quæ repugnantia, cùm nascatur ex aliqua oppositione, & in omni oppositione includatur affirmatio & negatio, esse & non esse, sequitur impossibile absolutè dictum esse illud, quod includit simul esse, & non esse, id est, quod includit & implicat contradictionem: ut hominem non esse animal rationale; quæ autem implicant contradictionem, sunt absolutè impossibilia, & potentiæ nulli subjiciuntur; quare dicendum est, illud esse objectum potentiæ Divinæ, quod est possibile, ex habitudine terminorum, id est, quod repugnantiam & contradictionem non involvit, quæ nempe sunt absolutè possibilia, possunt fieri ex parte ipsorum, nisi sit defectus aliquis in causa, seu potentia activa, at in potentia Dei nullus est defectus, cùm sit infinitæ perfectionis: impossibilia verò ex repugnantia terminorum, non subjiciuntur Divinæ potentiæ, quia impossibilia Logica, nullius potentiæ sunt objectum, nedum Divinæ, & hoc, ut dictum supra, non ex defectu Dei, quod cogitare blasphemum, sed ex defectu rei. Impossibilia nempe talia, fieri nequeunt, quia esse nequeunt, cum cùm in suo esse ipsum non esse includant. Unde acutissimi Derodonis judicio, quæ implicant contradictionem, melius dicuntur fieri non posse, quàm dicere, Deum ea facere non posse. Vide Derodonem Pneumatica cap.II. Articulo X. idem planè judicium cum Derodone est Golæi, ex duplici ratione, Exercitat. p.66.
units.tr: We, with all the orthodox, deny both claims, even supernaturally, and this not because of any defect in God but because of a defect in the thing itself, since it utterly overturns the very nature of one body and its bodily presence. And first, we argue against the multilocation [πολυτοπίαν] of one numerically one body as follows. Whatever involves a contradiction cannot be even supernaturally. But the same numerically one body being at several places at once involves a contradiction. Therefore the same numerically one body being at several places at once cannot be even supernaturally. The truth of the major premise is plain: what involves a contradiction, that is, contradictory predicates, is absolutely impossible, apart from any relation to some power, on account of the incompatibility of the terms. Since this incompatibility arises from some opposition, and every opposition includes affirmation and negation, being and not-being, it follows that what includes at once being and not-being, that is, what includes and implies a contradiction, is absolutely impossible, as for example that a man is not a rational animal. Things that imply a contradiction are absolutely impossible and are subject to no power. Hence we must say that what is the object of divine power is what is possible from the relation of the terms, that is, what does not involve incompatibility or contradiction. Such things are absolutely possible and can be made, on their own side, unless there is some defect in the cause or active power. But in God's power there is no defect, since it is of infinite perfection. Impossibilities arising from the incompatibility of terms, however, are not subject to divine power, since logical impossibilities are the object of no power whatever, much less of divine power. And this, as said above, is not because of a defect in God (to think so would be blasphemous) but because of a defect in the thing. Such impossibilities cannot come about because they cannot be, since in their very being they include non-being. Hence, by the judgment of the most acute Derodon, things that imply a contradiction are better said not to be able to be done than to say that God cannot do them. See Derodon, Pneumatica, chap. II, art. X. Golaeus, for two reasons, holds exactly the same judgment as Derodon, Exercitat., p. 66.

units.la: Minor probatur: quod destruit naturam unius corporis, illud de uno corpore affirmatum involvit contradictionem: sed πολυτοπία unius corporis, unius corporis destruit naturam. Ergo unum numero corpus esse in pluribus locis involvit contradictionem. Major constat: Minor probatur de destructione Logica hoc modo: Quicquid unum corpus dicit non unum, illud unius corporis destruit naturam. Sed πολυτοπία unius corporis, unum corpus dicit non unum. E. &c. Majoris veritas patet: Minor probatur: Quicquid unum numero corpus dicit à se ipso divisum, illud unum corpus dicit non unum. Sed πολυτοπία unius corporis, unum numero corpus dicit à se ipso divisum. Ergo &c. Major constat quia unum est, quod est indivisum in se, &à se; quicquid ergo dicit unum esse à se divisum, illud unum corpus dicit non unum; unum quidem in hypothesi, non unum verò ex consequentia. Minor; quia unum corpus, dico ita ex hypothesi adversariorum, non potest esse simul in pluribus locis sine divisione, & distantia à se ipso.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved as follows. What destroys the nature of one body, the affirmation of that thing of one body involves a contradiction. But multilocation [πολυτοπία] of one body destroys the nature of one body. Therefore one numerically one body being at several places involves a contradiction. The major premise is clear. The minor is proved thus, concerning logical destruction: whatever says that one body is not one destroys the nature of one body. But multilocation of one body says that one body is not one. Therefore etc. The truth of the major is plain. The minor is proved: whatever says that one numerically one body is divided from itself says that one body is not one. But multilocation of one body says that one numerically one body is divided from itself. Therefore etc. The major is clear, because one is that which is undivided in itself and from itself; whatever therefore says that one is divided from itself says that one body is not one, one indeed by hypothesis, but not one by consequence. The minor: because one body, as I say on the hypothesis of our opponents, cannot be at several places at once without division and distance from itself.

units.la: Hic quidem latibula quaerunt Adversarii in quibusdam nullius momenti distinctionibus, quas tamen non magis, quàm è pelvi fulmina metuimus, quippe quibus nē hilum proficiunt. Vide Physicam Derodonis part.1.tract.II.cap.II. Gorlæi Exercitat.p.212. Burgersdicii Collegium physicum, p.56.
units.tr: Here our adversaries seek hiding places in certain distinctions of no weight, which, however, we fear no more than thunderbolts from a basin, since they gain not the least ground. See Derodon, Physica, part I, tract. II, chap. II; Gorlaeus, Exercitat., p. 212; Burgersdicius, Collegium physicum, p. 56.

units.la: Quid de ubiquitate corporis Christi sentiendum sit, scholis Theologorum relinquimus decidendum; nobis idem de eo est judicium; qui præsentiam corporis Christi realem in Coena negamus, & pernegamus, præsentiam tantum sacramentalem & spiritualem agnoscentes. Vide Censuram ubiquitatis, seu confutationem argumentorum ubiquitariorum, M.Iohannis Lampadii; Metaphysicam Clarissimi D.VVirzii nostri cap.XVI.
units.tr: What should be thought of the ubiquity of the body of Christ we leave to be decided in the schools of the theologians. Our own judgment on it is this: we deny, and utterly deny, a real presence of Christ's body in the Supper, acknowledging only a sacramental and spiritual presence. See the Censure of Ubiquity, or refutation of the arguments of the ubiquitarians, by Master Johannes Lampadius; and our most distinguished Dr. Wirzius's Metaphysics, chap. XVI.

units.la: II. Plurium numero corporum μονοτοπίαν similiter ut nugacem, & sacræ Scripturæ, saniorique Philosophiæ injuriam negamus, unico hoc argumento: quòd μονοτοπία plurium numero corporum statuat corporum penetrationem, quàm nos impossibilem asserimus, cùm destruat naturam quantitatis, quæ requirit habentiam partis extra partem, seu positionem partium loco & spatio divisitam. Quid interea de inepta Iesuitarum, in extensionem internam & externam cantilena sentiendum, doctissimè ostendunt: Derodon thesibus de quantitate; item Physicæ part.I.tract.II.cap.II. Articulo III. Burgersd. Colleg.Phys.p.54.
units.tr: II. Similarly, we deny the single-placeness [μονοτοπίαν] of several numerically distinct bodies as trivial and as an injury to holy Scripture and to sounder philosophy, on this single argument: that the single-placeness of several numerically distinct bodies posits the penetration of bodies, which we declare impossible, since it destroys the nature of quantity, which requires that one part be outside another, that is, a position of parts divided by place and space. What should be thought meanwhile of the silly singsong of the Jesuits about internal and external extension, the most learned men have clearly shown: Derodon, theses on quantity; likewise Physica, part I, tract. II, chap. II, art. III; Burgersdicius, Collegium physicum, p. 54.

units.la: EX METAPHYSICA.
units.tr: FROM METAPHYSICS.

units.la: QUÆSTIO I. An Ens respectu Dei, & creaturæ, substantiæ & accidentis sit univocum?
units.tr: QUESTION I. Is Being, with respect to God and creature, substance and accident, univocal?

units.la: Pendet hæc quæstio verè ex alia, quæ inter literatos hodierno die ita agitari solet: An Ens habeat unum conceptum formalem, & unum conceptum objectivum, cujus nos affirmativam tuemur. Quid sit Entis conceptus formalis & objectivus, vide apud Suarezium Disp. Metaph. II. pag. 45. 46. Agnoscimus nos unum conceptum objectivum Entis, non tamen realiter unum unitate propriè dicta, sed tantùm unitate similitudinis, & conformitatis, cùm realiter dicat omnia Entia, omnia autem Entia sunt plura, licèt conveniant in ratione Entis, attamen iste conceptus non est realiter præcisus à propriis rationibus inferiorum, puta Dei & creaturæ, substantiæ & accidentis, quia de iis affirmativè prædicatur. Ex hoc multi opinantur, quòd Ens habeat unum conceptum formalem, & propriè dictum, qui quodlibet Ens inadæquatè repræsentet, & unum conceptum objectivum, unitate saltem conformitatis, Ens esse purè univocum, ut ita unum tantùm omnium prædicamentum exsculpant, inter quos sunt, Scotus, in 2. sent. dist. 3. quæst. 1. & 3. cum omnibus suis discipulis. De Raconis, Philosophus Gallus, Log. tractat. II. Quæst. II. artic. II. p. 178. Rodericus de Arriaga. Disput. Log. XI. p. 136. &c.
units.tr: This question really depends on another, which is commonly debated among scholars today: whether Being has one formal concept and one objective concept, and we defend the affirmative. For what the formal and objective concepts of Being are, see Suárez, Metaph. Disp. II, pp. 45–46. We acknowledge one objective concept of Being, but not one thing that is one by strictly so-called unity. It is one only by unity of likeness and conformity, since Being really signifies all beings, and all beings are many, though they agree in the notion of Being. Yet this concept is not really separated from the proper notions of its inferiors, namely God and creature, substance and accident, because it is predicated affirmatively of them. From this many think that Being has one formal and strictly so-called concept, which represents any being inadequately, and one objective concept with unity at least of conformity; and that Being is purely univocal, so that they carve out only one predicament of all things. Among these are Scotus, in 2 Sent. dist. 3 q. 1 and 3, with all his disciples; De Raconis, the French philosopher, Logic tract. II q. II art. II p. 178; Rodericus de Arriaga, Disp. Log. XI p. 136, and others.

units.la: Nos paucis ita rem explicamus. Dicimus I. Univocum esse vel univocans, vel univocatum. Univocum univocans est natura superior, quæ est pluribus communis, sub una & eadem ratione, & indifferenter ea respicit. Univocum univocatum, dicitur unumquodque ex illis, quibus prædicta natura superior est communis.
units.tr: We explain the matter briefly. First, we say that a univocal is either univocating or univocated. The univocating univocal is a superior nature common to many under one and the same notion, which regards them indifferently. The univocated univocal is each of those things to which the superior nature is common.

units.la: Dicimus II. Illam rationem tantùm eandem dici, quæ indifferenter respicit ea, quibus est communis, & æqualiter prædicatur de singulis, sine dependentia essentiali unius ab alio. Unde ratio significata per nomen analogum, non est eadem simpliciter, sed partim eadem, partim diversa. Eadem quidem, quatenus communis, diversa, quia non est indifferenter communis, & quia non convenit æqualiter ipsis, quibus est communis, quatenus participant nomen significans naturam communem.
units.tr: Second, we say that a notion is the same only when it regards indifferently those to which it is common, and is predicated equally of each, without essential dependence of one on another. Hence the notion signified by an analogous name is not simply the same, but partly the same and partly different. It is the same insofar as it is common, and different because it is not common indifferently, and because it does not belong equally to those to which it is common, insofar as they share in the name signifying the common nature.

units.la: Dicimus III. Univoca etiam à Philosophis distingui in Physica, Metaphysica, & Logica. Physica, quæ æqualiter participant naturam communem, adeò ut eam non contrahant perfectiori differentia, sed æquali, ut individua respectu speciei. Metaphysica, quæ inæqualiter participant naturam communem, adeò ut per perfectiorem & imperfectiorē differentiam eam contrahant, sine dependen-dendentia tamen unius ab altero, ut species resp. generis, puta homo & equus resp. animalis, quae univoca Metaphysica ab aliis dicuntur analoga physica, & analoga inaequalilatis. Logica, quae participant naturam communem cum dependentia unius inferioris ab alio, sic Deus & creatura possunt dici univoca Logica resp. Entis. Haec autem univoca Logica, aliter dicuntur Analoga Metaphysica. Vide Derodonem.
units.tr: Third, philosophers distinguish univocals into physical, metaphysical and logical. Physical univocals are those which participate equally in the common nature, so that they do not contract it by a more perfect difference but by an equal one, as individuals with respect to their species. Metaphysical univocals are those which participate unequally in the common nature, so that they contract it through a more perfect and a less perfect difference, yet without dependence of one on the other, as species with respect to their genus, for example man and horse with respect to animal. Others call these metaphysical univocals physical analogues, or analogues of inequality. Logical univocals are those which share the common nature with dependence of one inferior on another; so God and creature may be called logical univocals with respect to Being. These logical univocals are otherwise called metaphysical analogues. See Derodon.

units.la: Dicimus IV. Analoga etiam eadem ratione à Phylosophis distingui in Physica, & Metaphysica. Physica coincidunt cum univocis Metaphysicis, atque adeo sunt genera respectu specierum; Analoga Metaphysica coincidunt cum univocis purè logicis, qualia sunt transcendentia, quibus alii addunt Analoga Logica, quae coincidunt cum analogis extrinsecis.
units.tr: Fourth, by the same reasoning philosophers also distinguish analogues into physical and metaphysical. Physical analogues coincide with metaphysical univocals, and so are genera with respect to species. Metaphysical analogues coincide with purely logical univocals, such as the transcendentals, to which others add logical analogues, which coincide with extrinsic analogues.

units.la: Dicimus V. Analoga etiam à Philosophis dividi in intrinseca, & extrinseca. Intrinseca, in quibus omnibus ratio analoga reperitur proprie actu & formaliter, cum dependentia tamen essentiali unius ab alio, ut Ens resp. Dei & creaturae, substantiae, & accidentis. Extrinseca verò sunt, quando ratio analoga reperitur proprie actu & formaliter in uno, scilicet in primario analogato, in aliis vero improprie tantum, ut sanum quod convenit proprie soli animali, improprie urinae, medicamento.
units.tr: Fifth, philosophers also divide analogues into intrinsic and extrinsic. Intrinsic analogues are those in which the analogous notion is found in all of them properly, actually and formally, yet with essential dependence of one on another, as Being with respect to God and creature, or substance and accident. Extrinsic analogues are those in which the analogous notion is found properly, actually and formally in only one, namely the primary analogate, while in the others it is found only improperly, as "healthy" belongs properly only to the animal, and improperly to urine and to medicine.

units.la: His suppositis, respondemus I. Praesentem quaestione non esse de univoco univocato, sed de univoco univocante, & sic sensus illius est, utrum Ens prout est objectum adaequatum Metaphysicae, seu sub illa ratione formali, sub qua consideratur in Metaphysica, ita habeat rationem superioris communis, ut ratio significata per ipsum nomen Ens, sit una & eadem.
units.tr: With these points assumed, we answer first: the present question is not about the univocated univocal but about the univocating univocal. So its sense is this: whether Being, as it is the adequate object of metaphysics, or under that formal aspect under which it is considered in metaphysics, has the character of a common superior, such that the notion signified by the name Being itself is one and the same.

units.la: Respondemus II. Ens respectu Dei, & creaturae, substantiae & accidentis, non esse pure univocum, nec pure aequivocum, sed analogum, & analogum quidem intrinsecum, quia descensus Entis ad inferiora, non est uniformis, cum prius de uno dicatur, quam de altero, & unum inferius participet rationem Entis dependenter ab alio, idque dependentia essentiali, cum creatura essentialiter à Deo dependeat, item Accidens à substantia, cujus esse est actu inesse. Univocum quidem nec Physicum, eo quod ratio Entis resp. Dei & creaturae, substantiae & accidentis non contrahatur aequaliter, seu aequè perfecte ad ea, sed differentia perfectiori & imperfectiori: Nec univocum Metaphysicum, quia inferiora, licet participent rationem Entis inaequaliter, seu perfectiori & imperfectiori differentia, non tamen sine dependentia essentiali unius ab alio, quod tamen ad univocationem Metaphysicam requiritur.
units.tr: Second, we answer that Being with respect to God and creature, substance and accident is neither purely univocal nor purely equivocal, but analogous, and indeed intrinsically analogous. The descent of Being to its inferiors is not uniform, since it is predicated of one before the other, and one inferior participates in the notion of Being dependently on the other, and that by essential dependence, since the creature depends essentially on God, and likewise accident on substance, whose being is to inhere. It is not physically univocal, because the notion of Being is not contracted equally, or equally perfectly, to God and creature, substance and accident, but by a more perfect and a less perfect difference. Nor is it metaphysically univocal, because although the inferiors participate in the notion of Being unequally, that is by a more and a less perfect difference, they do not do so without essential dependence of one on another, which nevertheless metaphysical univocation requires.

units.la: Dicimus ergo Ens resp. Dei & creaturae, substantiae & accidentis esse Analogum Metaphysicum intrinsecum, in cujus inferioribus ratio analoga reperitur proprie & formaliter, cum dependentia tamen essentiali unius ab alio, & secundùm hoc analoga non tantum habent idem nomen, sed secundùm illud nomen, etiam unum conceptum, & unam rationem formalem, & definitionem;
units.tr: We say therefore that Being with respect to God and creature, substance and accident, is an intrinsic metaphysical analogue, in whose inferiors the analogous notion is found properly and formally, yet with essential dependence of one on another. Accordingly, analogues not only have the same name, but also, according to that name, one concept, one formal notion and one definition.

units.la: Vnde fit,ut Analogum hoc Metaphysicum intrinsecum, univocum saltem Logicum,non tamen purè univocum,quia ratio illa communis inæqualiter ab inferioribus participatur,dici posit; ad puram autem univocationem non requiritur dependentia essentialis unius inferioris ab alio,in qua nos rationem formalem analogorum positam esse existimamus. Atque hæc ita clara sunt, ut ei, qui hoc negotium,superius datis distinctionibus perspectis, non intelligat, præter helleborum remedii nihil superesse persuasum habeamus.
units.tr: Hence it follows that this intrinsic metaphysical analogue may be called univocal at least logically, but not purely univocal, because that common notion is participated in unequally by its inferiors. Pure univocation, however, does not require essential dependence of one inferior on another, and we hold that this dependence is the formal ground of analogues. These points are so clear that we are persuaded that anyone who, having grasped the distinctions given above, does not understand this matter has nothing left but hellebore as a remedy.

units.la: Nec sunt hic obiectiones de Raconis, quæ contra hanc nostram assertionem,pondus aliquod habeant,quas tamen firmissimas,in quibus omnia adversariorum propugnacula convulsa, & funditus eversa sint,thrasonicè somniatur Logicæ tract.II.p.178. Ita philosophandi ansam nactus ex Suarezio Disp.Metaph.II.sect.II.pag.49. quod tamen paulò inferius ipse solvit Suarez.p.59. & sequentibus.
units.tr: Nor are De Raconis's objections, which he raises against this our assertion, of any weight. He boastfully dreams that they are so firm that all the bulwarks of his opponents are shaken and utterly overthrown (Logic tract. II p. 178). He took the occasion for this philosophizing from Suárez, Disp. Metaph. II sect. II p. 49, which Suárez himself nevertheless resolves a little further on, at p. 59 and following.

units.la: Ita autem cornua obvertit de Raconis: Ens respectu Dei & creaturæ,substantiæ & accidentis habet ea omnia, quæ ad perfectam rationem synonymi exiguntur: Ergo eorum resp.est verè & proprie synonymum. Antecedens probat: Entis nomen est commune Deo & creaturis, substantiæ,& accidenti; rationem vero tali nomine significatam eis communem esse, hoc modo convincitur: quia ratio Entis talis est, ut sit aliquid reale distinctum à nihilo, & independens ab omni cogitatione intellectus; Atqui talis ratio convenit tam Deo, quàm creaturæ,tam substantiæ,quàm accidenti,eò quòd sint Entia realia.
units.tr: De Raconis turns his horns thus: Being with respect to God and creature, substance and accident, has all the things required for the perfect notion of a synonym; therefore with respect to them it is truly and properly a synonym. He proves the antecedent thus: the name Being is common to God and creatures, substance and accident; and that the notion signified by such a name is common to them is shown as follows: the notion of Being is such that it is something real, distinct from nothing and independent of every thought of the intellect. But such a notion belongs as much to God as to creature, as much to substance as to accident, since they are real beings.

units.la: Verùm respondeo I. ad argumentum de Raconis. Præterquam quòd petat principium, ludere æquivocatione in termino univoci,dum univocum Logicum,cùm univoco purè sic dicto confundat: Concedo nempe univoci esse Logici,habere idem nomen,& secundùm illud nomen,aliquam communem naturam participatam etiam cum dependentia unius inferioris ab alio: at nego hoc competere univoco purè sic dicto, quod requirit æqualitatem participationis superioris ab inferioribus,sine dependentia unius ab alio,ut superius. Univocationem Logicam sibi habeat, univocationem purè sic dictam nunquam obtinebit.
units.tr: But first I answer De Raconis's argument. Besides begging the question, he plays on an equivocation in the term univocal, confusing the logical univocal with the univocal purely so called. I grant that the logical univocal has the same name, and according to that name some common nature participated also with dependence of one inferior on another. But I deny that this belongs to the univocal purely so called, which requires an equality of participation of the superior by its inferiors, without dependence of one on another, as stated above. Let him keep logical univocation; he will never obtain univocation purely so called.

units.la: Respondeo II. Quæstionem hic esse de univoco puro,& proprie sic dicto, quod nos constituimus in æqualitate,& independentia unius inferioris ab alio: Ergo vel Raconem, cum suo univoco Logico ignorare Elenchum,vel si intelligat de purè univoco,ipsius argumenti negamus antecedens, & probationem ridiculam dicimus,quia fumum vendat, cùm requisita perfectè univoci omittat, quæ nos ponimus independentiam,& æqualitatem participationis.
units.tr: I answer, second: the question here concerns the pure univocal, properly so called, which we locate in the equality and independence of one inferior from another. So either Raco, with his logical univocal, is ignoring the elenchus, or, if he means the purely univocal, we deny the antecedent of his argument itself and call his proof ridiculous, because he is peddling smoke, since he leaves out the requisites of the perfectly univocal, which we hold to be independence and equality of participation.

units.la: Respondeo III. In probatione argumenti de Raconis medium terminum, seu hæc verba,ratio Entis convenit tam Deo, quàm creaturis, tam substantiæ, quàm accidenti,esse ambigua. Vel enim absolutè sumpta nihil probant, cùm tota quæstio de convenientia seu communicatione æquali à nobis instituatur, in qua nos rationem formalem univoci purè & proprié sic dicti ponimus: Vel si comparatè ad sua inferiora communicatio de æquali, & inæquali intelligatur, distinguimus: Eadem est ratio Entis in inferioribus specie & secundùm terminum realiter concedo, at secundùm participationem Entis nego; licèt autem ratio Entis comparatè ad inferiora esset una specie, per unitatem conformitatis, quæ inter ea invenitur, non tamen esset purè univoca, quia non est uniformis, eò quòd inferiora participent rationem Entis inæqualiter, & cum dependentia essentiali unius ab alio, quæ dependentia tollit puram univocationem, & constituit analogiam.
units.tr: I answer, third: in the proof of Raco's argument, the middle term, or these words, "the notion of being belongs equally to God and creatures, to substance and accident," is ambiguous. Taken absolutely, they prove nothing, since our whole question concerns agreement or communication on an equal footing, in which we posit the formal ground of the univocal purely and properly so called. Or, if communication of equal and unequal is understood comparatively to its inferiors, we distinguish. The notion of being is the same in species and, as to the term, I grant it really; but as to the participation of being, I deny it. Even if the notion of being compared with its inferiors were one in species, through the unity of conformity found among them, it would still not be purely univocal, because it is not uniform: the inferiors participate in the notion of being unequally, and with an essential dependence of one on another. This dependence removes pure univocity and constitutes analogy.

units.la: Sed instat de Raconis p. 179. Entis essentia omnino est æqualiter in omnibus inferioribus; quia nihil magis habet in uno, quàm in aliis, cùm dicat unum gradum indivisibilem, & non ex multis gradibus compositum.
units.tr: But he insists, from Raco, p. 179: the essence of being is wholly equal in all its inferiors, because it has nothing more in one than in the others, since it is one indivisible degree and not composed of many degrees.

units.la: Respondeo I. Falsum esse Ens esse in inferioribus Deo, & creatura, substantia, & accidente æquale, cùm contrahatur ad ea differentia perfectiori & imperfectiori; quæ differentiæ, cùm intrinsecè ab Ente non distinguantur, utique Ens in inferioribus æquale esse non potest. Adde quod Divinæ Majestati est injurium, Entis rationem in Deo æquiparare Enti creato, cùm in Deo esse sit per essentiam, in creaturis tantùm per participationem; in Deo enim esse eminenter in creaturis formaliter, quæ ni inæqualitatem in participatione Entis inferant, quid inferre possit non video.
units.tr: I answer, first: it is false that being is equal in its inferiors, God and creature, substance and accident, since it is contracted to them by the differences of more perfect and less perfect. Since these differences are not intrinsically distinct from being, being cannot possibly be equal in its inferiors. Add that it is injurious to the Divine Majesty to equate the notion of being in God with created being, since in God to be is through essence, and in creatures only through participation. For to be in God is eminently what in creatures is formally; and unless these imply inequality in the participation of being, I do not see what they could imply.

units.la: Respondeo II. Indivisibile esse duplex. Absolutè, & secundùm quid. Absolutè, quod prorsus non potest dividi in plura, ut punctum: secundùm quid, cùm quid, licèt divisibile, non potest ita dividi, ut maneat idem adæquatè cum se ipso indiviso secundùm rem & rationem, qui posterior tantùm modus, quoad indivisibilitatem Logicam, Enti convenire potest.
units.tr: I answer, second: indivisible is twofold, absolutely and in a certain respect. It is absolutely indivisible what cannot at all be divided into many, like a point. It is indivisible in a certain respect when a thing, though divisible, cannot be divided so as to remain adequately the same as itself undivided, in thing and in notion. Only this latter mode can belong to being, as regards logical indivisibility.

units.la: Postremò de Raconis probare conatur, ad puram univocationem indepen-dentiam essentialem non requiri hac ratione; quia quilibet habitus dependeat à facultate naturali, cui insidet: atqui facultati & habitibus qualitatem convenire univocè. E. ad rationem univoci non requiri independentiam.
units.tr: Lastly, Raco tries to prove that essential independence is not required for pure univocation, by this reasoning: every habit depends on the natural faculty in which it inheres; but quality belongs univocally to faculties and to habits; therefore independence is not required for the notion of the univocal.

units.la: Respondeo I. ad majorem: laborare eam homonymia in vocabulo dependere. Alia enim est dependentia essentialis, in participatione alicujus attributi; alia accidentalis ex subordinatione causarum. Sola autem dependentia hæc essentialis participati va unius alicujus attributi invehit analogiam. Dependentia autem effectus à causa, præterquam à prima, non essentialis, sed accidentalis est; ac proinde ratio Raconis ignorat Elenchum.
units.tr: I answer, first, to the major premise: it labours under an equivocation in the word "dependence." One dependence is essential, in the participation of some attribute; another is accidental, arising from the subordination of causes. Only this essential dependence, in the participation of one attribute, introduces analogy. The dependence of an effect on a cause other than the first is not essential but accidental. Consequently Raco's argument ignores the elenchus.

units.la: Respondeo II. falsum esse, qualitatem convenire facultati & habitibus univocè; Cùm nempe facultates, sint proprietates rei, à qua intrinsecè non distinguuntur, qualitas de iis non nisi æquivocè prædicari potest.
units.tr: I answer, second: it is false that quality belongs univocally to faculties and habits. Since faculties are properties of the thing from which they are not intrinsically distinct, quality can be predicated of them only equivocally.

units.la: QUÆSTIO II.
units.tr: QUESTION II.

units.la: An essentiæ rerum creatarum sint æternæ?
units.tr: Are the essences of created things eternal?

units.la: In negativam vergimus, cum acutissimo Derodone, qui thesibus de hac materia in lucem editis, & tractatu subtilissimo contra Atheos, p.56.57. Disputatione item de universali in communi, pag. 89.90. & seq. solidissimé, ut solidius viderim nihil, eam pertractat. Rationes autem hæ sunt: I. Æternitas includit essentialiter durationem, & duratio includit essentialiter existentiam; at essentiæ rerum creatarum non habent existentiam ab æterno. Ergo essentiæ rerum creatarum non sunt æternæ. II. Essentia rei est ipsa res, cùm res definiatur per essentiam. Sed res creatæ non sunt æternæ, ut omnes fatentur Orthodoxi, aliter enim dicere implicaret. Ergo essentiæ rerum non sunt æternæ. III. Æternitas positiva est attributum Dei incommunicabile creaturæ; Ergo essentia rerum creatarum æterna esse nequit. IV. Æternum est improductum; at essentiæ rerum creatarum non sunt improductæ; sic enim essent Entia à se, independentia ab omni alio, ac consequenter ipse Deus. Ergo essentiæ rerum creatarum non sunt æternæ. V. Si essentiæ rerum creatarum essent æternæ, sequeretur creaturas non esse factas ex nihilo, atque adeò nou esse creatas; at creaturas non esse factas ex nihilo tam sui, quàm subjecti, atque adeò non esse creatas, hæreticum.
units.tr: We incline to the negative with the most acute Derodon, who treats this matter very solidly in his theses published on the subject and in his most subtle treatise against the Atheists, pp. 56–57, and likewise in his Disputation on the universal in general, pp. 89–90 and following. I have seen nothing more solid. His arguments are these. I. Eternity essentially includes duration, and duration essentially includes existence; but the essences of created things do not have existence from eternity. Therefore the essences of created things are not eternal. II. The essence of a thing is the thing itself, since a thing is defined through its essence. But created things are not eternal, as all orthodox writers admit, for to say otherwise would be contradictory. Therefore the essences of things are not eternal. III. Positive eternity is an attribute of God that cannot be communicated to a creature. Therefore the essence of a created thing cannot be eternal. IV. What is eternal is unproduced; but the essences of created things are not unproduced, for then they would be beings from themselves, independent of everything else, and consequently God himself. Therefore the essences of created things are not eternal. V. If the essences of created things were eternal, it would follow that creatures were not made out of nothing, and so were not created; but to say that creatures were not made out of nothing, both as to their own being and as to their subject, and so were not created, is heretical.

units.la: Ad hanc rationem excipiunt adversarii, omnia facta ex nihilo existentiæ, sed non ex nihilo essentiæ. Cui sufficienter respondet Suarezius Disput. XXXI. sect. II p.159. Nos respondemus ratione sequenti.
units.tr: Our opponents answer this argument by saying that all things were made out of nothing as to their existence, but not out of nothing as to their essence. Suarez answers this sufficiently in Disputation XXXI, section II, p. 159. We reply with the following argument.

units.la: VI. Essentia & existentia rerum creatarum realiter intrinsecé non distinguuntur. Ergo essentia non potest esse æterna sine existentia. Vi harum rationum perspecta, adversarii evadere conantur distinctione inter essentiam actualem & posssibilem: & rationes has veras dicunt de essentia actuali, non autem de possibili; Essentiam nempe possibilem, seu possibilitatem essentiæ, non esse productam, & consequenter esse æternam.
units.tr: VI. The essence and existence of created things are not really or intrinsically distinct. Therefore the essence cannot be eternal without existence. Having grasped the force of these arguments, our opponents try to escape them by distinguishing between actual and possible essence. They say that the arguments are true of actual essence but not of possible essence, namely that the possible essence, or the possibility of an essence, has not been produced and consequently is eternal.

units.la: Respondetur: Præter id, quòd essentiæ possibilitas dici debeat improducta negativé, non privativé, cùm productio tantùm terminetur, nec aliter terminari possit, nisi in actualitate possibilitati opposita, (ignoscant Ciceroniani manes, si quid liberius delicatas eorum aures, philosophica obtundimus barbarie, audiant Scaligerum: Qua ratione vocabulis scholasticorum, licét barbaris, tempestivé uti nequeamus non video. Non enim in foro versamur, aut Romano consilio, sed in communi theatro sapientum, sub oculis veritatis, cujus suppellectilem atque apparatum, non tam nitidum, quàm opulentum esse decet. Scaliger Exercit. I. sect. 1, p.3.) nec essentiam possibilem esse æternam, idque Logicè
units.tr: We reply: apart from the fact that the possibility of an essence ought to be called unproduced in a negative sense, not a privative one, since production is terminated only in actuality, and cannot terminate otherwise than in actuality opposed to possibility (let the shades of Cicero forgive me if, with philosophical barbarity, I offend their dainty ears a little more freely; let them hear Scaliger: I do not see why we cannot use the terms of the scholastics, though barbarous, when they are needed. For we are not working in the forum or in Roman counsel, but in the common theatre of the wise, under the eyes of truth, whose furnishings and equipment ought to be not so much elegant as abundant. Scaliger, Exercitationes I, section 1, p. 3), nor is the possible essence eternal, either logically

units.la: Physicé. Cùm enim possibile nihil aliud sit, quàm quod actu potest existere, certé si essentia possibilis esset æterna, sequeretur, essentiam posse actu existere ab æterno; at hoc esse non potest; sic nempe creaturæ essent æternæ, seu existe-rent ab æterno, cùm essentia rei sit ipsa res, at hoc absurdum. Si verò creaturæ non possunt existere ab æterno, illorum essentia actu non potest existere ab æ-terno, siqué essentia creaturæ non est possibilis ab æterno.
units.tr: or physically. For since the possible is nothing other than what can actually exist, certainly if the possible essence were eternal, it would follow that the essence could actually exist from eternity; but this cannot be. For in that case creatures would be eternal, or would exist from eternity, since the essence of a thing is the thing itself; and this is absurd. If, on the other hand, creatures cannot exist from eternity, then their essence cannot actually exist from eternity, and so the essence of a creature is not possible from eternity.

units.la: Non quidem possibilitate Logica, cùm nempe illa sit in sola nonrepugnan-tia, seu noninvolutione prædicatorum contradictoriorum, sequitur eò ipso, quòd repugnet rei essentiam esse æternam, cùm omne Ens præter Deum re-pugnet esse ab æterno, ipsius possibilitatem, seu non repugnantiam non esse æ-ternam. Non etiam Physica, quia si possibilitas Physica, id est, producibilitas rei esset æterna, res esset producibilis ab æterno, sicque posset existere ab ѕterno, quod absurdum.
units.tr: Not logically, since logical possibility lies solely in non-repugnance, or the non-involution of contradictory predicates; it does not follow from this, because it is repugnant for a thing's essence to be eternal, since every being except God is repugnant to being from eternity, that its possibility, or non-repugnance, is not eternal. Nor physically, because if the physical possibility, that is, the producibility of a thing, were eternal, the thing would be producible from eternity, and so could exist from eternity, which is absurd.

units.la: Mitius paulò de hac possibili essentiarum ɛternitate statuunt, qui existi-mant, essentias illas, seu esse essentiæ ex parte creaturæ, antequam à Deo produ-cantur, non esse aliquam rem distinctam à Deo, quæ sit simpliciter extra nihil, sed ex parte creaturæ, dicere rantùm aptitudinem quandam, seu potius non re-pugnantiam, ut in tali esse à Deo producantur; & in hoc distingui essentias re-rum creatarum, à rebus fictitiis, & impossibilibus Logicé; & hòc seusu dici crea-turas habere reales essentias, etiamsi non existant, dici autem habere non actu, sed potestate, non per potentiam intrinsecam, sed extrinsecam creatòris, atque ita dici habere esse non in se, sed in causa sua, quòd ab æterno ab hac causa fuerint producibiles, sicque aliqua ratione æternas dici posse; quam sententiam Capreo-lo attribuit Suarezius Disp. Metaph. XXXI. sect. 2, p. 159.
units.tr: More mildly, some hold something a little different about this possible eternity of essences. They think that those essences, or the being of the essence on the creature's side, before they are produced by God, are not some thing distinct from God that is simply outside nothing; rather, on the creature's side, they express only a certain aptitude, or rather a non-repugnance, to be produced by God in such a being; and in this the essences of created things are distinguished from fictitious things and things logically impossible. In this sense, they say, creatures are said to have real essences even though they do not exist, and are said to have being not actually but potentially, not through an intrinsic power but through the extrinsic power of the Creator. Thus they are said to have being not in themselves but in their cause, because they were producible from eternity by this cause, and so can in some way be called eternal. Suarez attributes this opinion to Capreolus, Disputation XXXI, Metaphysics, section 2, p. 159.

units.la: Respondeo I. possibilem essentiarum æternitatem, à sola denominatione extrinseca causæ efficientis, nequaquam posse adstrui; cùm hoc modo essentiæ creaturarum abesse Dei non distinguantur; at essentia Dei non est creatura, seu creata, sed tantùm creatrix.
units.tr: I reply, first, that the possible eternity of essences cannot be upheld on the basis of an extrinsic designation of the efficient cause alone, since in this way the essences of creatures would not be distinguished from the essence of God; yet the essence of God is not a creature, or created, but only creator.

units.la: Respondeo II.
