Ab æterno dari possibilitatem rei in tempore, eò quòd ab æterno nulla repugnantia, aut contradictio sit assignabilis, ut res existat in tem-pore; at negamus dari possibilitatem, seu nonrepugnantiam ab æterno, essentias illas esse ab æterno, quia aliquid præter Deum, seu ab essentia Dei distinctum es-se positivé æternum implicat contradictionem, ut dictum supra.
units.tr: I reply, second, that from eternity there is a possibility of a thing existing in time, because from eternity no repugnance or contradiction can be assigned to the thing's existing in time. But we deny that there is a possibility, or non-repugnance, from eternity that those essences are from eternity, because to be positively eternal, as something distinct from God, or from the essence of God, involves a contradiction, as was said above.

units.la: Respondet III. Acutissimus Derodon, distinguendum esse inter has duas propositiones; ab æterno res sunt, possibiles, producibiles, aut factibiles, & res res sunt possibiles, producibiles & factibiles ab æterno. Priorem propositionem esse verā, modò explicetur hoc pacto: ab æterno res sunt possibiles, producibi-les, aut factibiles in tempore, id est, ab æterno non repugnat res esse, producì aut fieri in tempore, & verum est, dicere ab æterno, quòd res sint possibiles, produ-cibiles, aut factibiles in tempore. Posteriorem verò propositionem, scil. res sunt possipossibiles, producibiles,& factibiles ab æterno, esse falsam, quia habet hunc sen- sum, res possunt existere, produci aut fieri ab æterno, quod contradictionem in- volvit.
units.tr: Derodon replies, III: one must distinguish between these two propositions: things are possible, producible, or feasible from eternity; and things are possible, producible, and feasible from eternity. The former proposition is true, provided it is explained thus: from eternity things are possible, producible, or feasible in time; that is, from eternity it is not repugnant for a thing to be, to be produced, or to be made in time, and it is true to say that from eternity things are possible, producible, or feasible in time. The latter proposition, namely that things are possible, producible, and feasible from eternity, is false, because it has this sense: things can exist, be produced, or be made from eternity, which involves a contradiction.

units.la: Respondet IV. Derodon, tractatu in Atheos p. 57, hanc propositionem, es- sentiæ rerum sunt possibiles ab æterno, vel essentiæ rerum sunt in potentia ab æterno, duas pati explicationes: Nam si esse ab æterno dicatur de vocabulo po- tentia, propositionem esse veram, ejusque sensum talem esse, potentia produ&ti- va essentiarum est ab æterno. Si vero referatur ad vocabulum essentiarum, esse falsam, essentiæ enim nec possunt, nec potuerunt esse ab æterno; & licèt ab æter- no essentiæ fuerint possibiles pro tempore, non tamen pro æterno. Vide plura loco citato, tractatu in Atheos, & paginis aliquot sequentibus. Vide etiam hujus controversiæ explicationem, solidam & succinctam, apud Myllerum Metaph. lib. I, c. 3 p. 14. & 15.
units.tr: Derodon replies, IV, in his treatise against the Atheists, p. 57, that the proposition "the essences of things are possible from eternity" or "the essences of things are in potency from eternity" admits of two explanations. For if "from eternity" is taken as applying to the word "potency," the proposition is true, and its sense is that the productive potency of essences is from eternity. But if it is referred to the word "essences," it is false, for essences neither can nor could be from eternity; and although the essences were possible from eternity in respect of time, they were not possible in respect of eternity. See more in the passage cited from the treatise against the Atheists, and in several following pages. See also the solid and concise explanation of this controversy in Müller, Metaphysics, book I, chapter 3, pp. 14–15.

units.la: QUÆSTIO III.
units.tr: QUESTION III.

units.la: An dentur Entia rationis objectiva tantùm?
units.tr: Are there beings of reason that are merely objective?

units.la: Antequam ad quæstionis hujus progrediamur solutionem, sequentia, quo veritas ita clarior evadat, præmonstrabimus. Dicimus ergo I. Cùm Ens rationis dicatur ex habitudine, quam habet ad rationem, juxta diversas habitudines seu varium est. Aliud enim in intellectu est subjectivè, & sic ei insunt quæ in ipso sunt, sicut accidentia in subjecto, v. g. scientiæ & actus ejus, quia intellectui insunt, sicut albedo corpori. Aliud effectivè, sicut effectus in causa, quomodo ea, quæ per intellectum efficiuntur, ipsi inesse dicuntur; sic omnes actiones mentis, item artefacta pertinent ad mentem. Aliud objectivè, quia nimirum ipsius est objectum, seu ad intellectum sese habet admodum objecti, quia per cognitio- nem intellectûs, intellectui aliquid actu objicitur; nam quia cognitio fit, quasi per attractionem rei cognitæ ad cognoscentem, dicitur res cognita esse in cogno- scente, non solùm inhæsivè per suam imaginem, sed etiam objectivè, secundùm se ipsam. Explicationem trium harum Entis rationis specierum, vide apud Suarezium Disp. Metaph. LIV. p. 701; Stahlium Metaph. p. 4, 5. Heereboordium Disput. select. p. 686, Scheibl. Metaph. lib. I, cap. XXVII. p. 405. Derodonem Disp. de Ente rationis thes. 1 & 2; Burgersd. Metaph. p. 30. Myllerum Metaph. p. 44. Ens rationis objectivum Combachius vocat comparativum, quòd fit ex operatione comparativa intellectus. Combachius Metaph. p. 143 & p. 149.
units.tr: Before we proceed to the solution of this question, we will set out the following points, so that the truth may become clearer. We say, therefore, I. Since a being of reason is so called from the relation it has to reason, it varies according to the different relations. For one thing is in the intellect subjectively, and so those things that are in it inhere in it as accidents in a subject, for example, sciences and their acts, which inhere in the intellect as whiteness inheres in a body. Another thing is in it effectively, as an effect is in its cause; in this way those things that are produced through the intellect are said to be in it, and so all actions of the mind, and likewise artefacts, belong to the mind. Another thing is in it objectively, namely because it is the object of the intellect, or stands towards the intellect as an object does, since through the cognition of the intellect something is actually presented to the intellect. For since cognition happens as it were by the attraction of the known thing to the knower, the known thing is said to be in the knower not only inherently through its image but also objectively, according to itself. For an explanation of these three species of being of reason, see Suarez, Disp. Metaph. LIV, p. 701; Stahl, Metaph. pp. 4, 5; Heereboord, Disput. select. p. 686; Scheibler, Metaph. lib. I, cap. XXVII, p. 405; Derodon, Disp. de Ente rationis, theses 1 and 2; Burgersdijk, Metaph. p. 30; Muller, Metaph. p. 44. Combach calls the objective being of reason comparative, because it arises from the comparative operation of the intellect. Combach, Metaph. pp. 143 and 149.

units.la: Dico II. Ens rationis effectivum & subjectivum, à prædictis authoribus, qui tamen majori ex parte Entis rationis sunt patroni, haberi verum Ens reale, ratione intrinseci, quia ei competant affectiones Entis realis, scilicet unitas, veri- tas, bonitas. Heereboord Disp. select. p. 686. Eadem mens est Suarezio loco citato.Myllero Metaph p.44.Burgersdicius propterea Entia realia dicenda putat, quòd habeant veram essentiam, & sint capacia verae realisq; existentiae. Metaph. p.3o.Et dici tantum Entia rationis ab extrinsecis
units.tr: I say II. A being of reason that is effective and subjective is held by the authors cited above, who nevertheless for the most part are defenders of beings of reason, to be a true real being by reason of what is intrinsic to it, because the affections of a real being belong to it, namely unity, truth and goodness. Heereboord, Disp. select. p. 686. Suarez, cited above, has the same view. Muller, Metaph. p. 44. Burgersdijk therefore thinks such things should be called real beings, because they have a true essence and are capable of true and real existence, Metaph. p. 30. And they are called beings of reason only on account of extrinsic...

units.la: Dico III. Eorum, quae sunt objectivè in intellectu, quaedam habere esse in se, id est, citra hoc quod cognoscuntur, habent vel habere possunt verum esse reale, secundum quod rationi objiciuntur; & haec absolutè & simpliciter, non sunt verum Ens rationis, sed reale, quia hoc esse est, quod simpliciter ac per se illis convenit, objici autem rationi, est illis extrinsecum tantum, & accidentarium. Quaedam habent solum esse objectivè, id est, praeter hoc quod cognoscuntur, nullum habent esse atque adeo totum eorum esse, nihil aliud est, quàm objici intellectui, seu rationi de illis cogitanti, & haec propriissimè vocantur Ens rationis, quia non habent alium nobiliorem, aut magis realem essendi modum, unde possint Ens appellari. E. G. Quando aliquid cognosco secus quàm est, neque objectum ita se habet, sicut in intellectu repraesentatur, tunc tantùm est objectivè in intellectu, & vocatur Ens rationis, v.gr. si dicam, Deus est ligneus, affirmo inter Deum esse, & ligneum esse identitatem. Illa identitas est tantùm objectivè in intellectu, quia ego quidem concipio Deum esse ligneum, sed in se, & citra mentis operationem illa identitas nulla est, cùm impossibile sit aliquid simul esse Deum & ligneum. Et haec dico ex hypothesi adversariorum; quia in nostra sententia, nihil potest concipi aliter, quàm est, nedum Deus ligneus, quia in intellectu involveret contradictionem, ut infra. Quando autem cognosco aliquid sicuti est, tunc illud non tantùm habet esse objectivum in intellectu, sed citra hoc, quòd objectum intellectus est, aliud esse habet, & sic nullum fit Ens rationis; ut, cùm dico, Deus est justus, mente percipio identitatem inter Deum & justum, vel justitiam, & sic identitas illa est objectivè in intellectu, sed praeter illud esse objectivum, habet illa identitas, esse reale in se, quia Deus & justitia ejus, sunt idem citra mentis operationem, seu nemine id cogitante.
units.tr: I say III. Of those things that are objectively in the intellect, some have being in themselves, that is, apart from being known they have, or can have, true real being, in accordance with which they are presented to reason. These, absolutely and simply, are not a true being of reason but a real one, because this being is what belongs to them simply and per se, whereas being presented to reason is extrinsic and merely accidental to them. Others have only objective being, that is, apart from being known they have no being at all, and so their whole being is nothing other than being presented to the intellect, or to reason thinking of them. These are most properly called beings of reason, because they have no other nobler or more real mode of being by which they could be called beings. For example, when I know something otherwise than it is, and the object does not stand as it is represented in the intellect, then it is only objectively in the intellect and is called a being of reason. If I say, "God is wooden," I affirm an identity between God and being wooden. That identity is only objectively in the intellect: I indeed conceive God to be wooden, but in itself, and apart from an operation of the mind, that identity does not exist, since it is impossible for something to be both God and wooden. I say this on the hypothesis of our opponents; for in our view nothing can be conceived otherwise than it is, much less God as wooden, since in the intellect it would involve a contradiction, as below. But when I know something as it is, then it not only has objective being in the intellect, but apart from being the object of the intellect it has another being, and so it is not a being of reason at all. For example, when I say, "God is just," I perceive by the mind an identity between God and the just, or justice. That identity is objectively in the intellect, but beyond that objective being it has real being in itself, because God and his justice are the same apart from any operation of the mind, or with no one thinking it.

units.la: Dico IV. Ens rationis proprie sic dictum, à Philosophis definiri; quod habet tantùm esse objectivè in intellectu, & extra intellectum est purum nihil; seu esse id, quod à ratione cogitatur ut Ens, cùm tamen in se entitatem non habeat: Quod Thomas opuscul.42.cap.1.explicat, fieri tunc, quando intellectus nititur apprehendere quod non est, & ideo fingit illud aliquo modo ut Ens; vide Suarezium Disput. LIV.p.702.
units.tr: I say IV. A being of reason, properly so called, is defined by the philosophers as that which has only objective being in the intellect and outside the intellect is pure nothing; or, that which reason thinks of as a being, though in itself it has no entity. Thomas explains this in Opusc. 42, cap. 1, as happening when the intellect strives to apprehend what is not, and therefore feigns it in some way as a being; see Suarez, Disp. LIV, p. 702.

units.la: Dico V. Ens reale contradistinctum huic Enti rationis esse illud, quod existit, sive existere potest, nemine cogitante de ipso. Dixi quod existere potest, posssibilitate scilicet Logica, quae consistit in nonrepugnantia, seu noninvolutione praedicatorum contradictoriorum, quod tam Enti actu existenti, quàm Enti potentiâ convenit.
units.tr: I say V. A real being, as distinguished from this being of reason, is that which exists, or can exist, whether or not anyone is thinking of it. I said "can exist," namely with logical possibility, which consists in the non-repugnance, or non-involution, of contradictory predicates, and which belongs equally to a being actually existing and to a being in potency.

units.la: Dico V. Ens reale sumi interdum participialiter, id est, ut participium verbi esse, & significat existentiam, seu rem actu existentem; interdum nominaliter, id est, vi nominis, & ut habetur pro nomine substantivo, & significat essentiam, seu rem excludentem praedicata contradictoria. Vide Hurtadum de Mendoza Disp. Metaph. II. sect. 1.
units.tr: I say V. A real being is sometimes taken participially, that is, as the participle of the verb "to be," and signifies existence, or a thing actually existing; sometimes nominally, that is, by force of the noun, taken as a substantive, and signifies essence, or a thing excluding contradictory predicates. See Hurtado de Mendoza, Disp. Metaph. II, sect. 1.

units.la: Dico VII. Aliter hanc distinctionem tradi in Ens actu, & Ens potentia. Ens actu, quod actu existit. Potentia vero, quod quidem non actu existit, sed potest existere. Ens vero potentia, tale est vel potentia physica, vel Logica. Potentia physica, quod non actu existit, sed potest existere. Potentia Logica, quod non repugnat esse, sive actu existat, sive non.
units.tr: I say VII. This distinction is drawn otherwise for being in act and being in potency. Being in act is that which actually exists. Being in potency is that which indeed does not actually exist, but can exist. Being in potency is either physical or logical. Physical potency is that which does not actually exist but can exist. Logical potency is that which does not repugn being, whether it actually exists or not.

units.la: Dico VIII. Ens reale esse tale, vel simpliciter & absolutè, vel tantum secundum quid: illud dicitur de Ente actu existente duntaxat: hoc vero etiam de non Ente actu existente, modo possit existere. Ex quo patet possibile physicè non esse Ens reale simpliciter & absolutè, sed tantum Ens reale diminutum & secundum quid; possibile vero Logicè, si actu existat, esse vere Ens reale, simpliciter & absolutè; at si actu non existat, esse tantum Ens reale diminutum, & secundum quid, contradictionem Enti rationis superius definito, quod tantum habet esse objectivum in intellectu, & extra intellectum est purum nihil, seu involvens contradictionem. Hinc liquet possibile, seu Ens potentia, posse esse nihil, aut non Ens purum, cum sit Ens diminutum, & secundum quid. Cum ergo Ens potentia sit reale saltem diminutum, Ens rationis objectivè tantum esse non potest.
units.tr: I say VIII. A real being is either such simply and absolutely, or only in a certain respect. The former is said only of a being actually existing, the latter also of a non-being that is actually existing, provided it can exist. From this it is plain that what is physically possible is not a real being simply and absolutely, but only a diminished real being, and in a certain respect. What is logically possible, if it actually exists, is truly a real being, simply and absolutely; but if it does not actually exist, it is only a diminished real being, and in a certain respect. This contradicts the being of reason defined above, which has only objective being in the intellect and outside the intellect is pure nothing, or which involves a contradiction. Hence it is clear that the possible, or being in potency, can be nothing, or pure non-being, since it is a diminished being, and in a certain respect. Since therefore being in potency is at least a diminished real being, a being of reason cannot be merely objective.

units.la: Dico IX. Ex mente adversariorum ea, quae habent esse objectivè tantum in intellectu duplicia esse: quaedam enim licet actu esse non habeant, possunt tamen habere, ut si parietem, qui albus est; dicam esse nigrum, identitas inter hujusmodi parietem & nigrum ab intellectu concipitur, & sic est objectivè in intellectu, sed reipsa non est actu, potest tamen esse, quia nihil repugnat parietem album fieri nigrum. Quaedam vero ne habere quidem possunt aliud esse, & talis est identitas inter Deum & ligneum esse, quod cum contradictionem implicet, per nullam potentiam fieri potest. Ita refert Stahlius Metaph. p. 6.
units.tr: I say IX. According to the opponents' view, those things that have being only objectively in the intellect have a twofold being. For some, although they do not have actual being, can yet have it: if I were to call a wall, which is white, black, the identity between such a wall and black is conceived by the intellect, and so it is objectively in the intellect; but in fact it is not actually so, yet it can be, since nothing prevents a white wall from becoming black. But some things cannot have any other being at all, and such is the identity between God and being wooden, which, since it implies a contradiction, cannot come about through any power. Thus Stahl reports, Metaph. p. 6.

units.la: His praenotatis respondeo: Cum objectum adaequatum intellectus sit Ens, & nihil possit concipere, nisi ad modum Entis, ut fusè explicat Suarezius Disp. Metaph LIV. pag. 702. At vero Entia rationis objectiva tantum, esse positivum non habeant, neque habere possint, sed tantum habeant per hoc, quod sunt objectum intellectus, ex sententia adversariorum, & concipiantur per modum rerum, & formarum positivarum, cum tamen tales in seipsis revera esse non possint, nulla dari Entia rationis objectiva tantum, seu talia, quae possint esse objectum intellectus citra esse in se, vel actu, vel potentia, constanter asserimus hoc argumento:
units.tr: Having set out these preliminaries, I answer: since the adequate object of the intellect is being (Ens), and the intellect can conceive nothing except in the mode of being, as Suarez explains at length (Disp. Metaph. LIV, p. 702). But beings of reason that are merely objective have no positive being, and cannot have it. They have only this much: they are the object of the intellect, according to our opponents, and they are conceived in the manner of things and positive forms, although such beings could not really exist in themselves. Therefore we constantly assert, with this argument, that there are no beings of reason that are merely objective, that is, such beings as could be the object of the intellect without existing in themselves, either actually or potentially:

units.la: Si daretur Ens rationis objectivum tantum, tum vel conciperetur non Ens, tanquam Ens, vel unum Ens tanquam aliud Ens, vel impossibile ad modum possibilis. At nec potest concipi non Ens, tanquam Ens, nec unum Ens, tanquam aliud Ens, nec impossibile ad modum possibilis. Ergo non datur Ens ra- tionis objectivum tantùm. Ratio consequentiæ: quia Ens rationis objectivum tantùm, seu objectum intelle-ctus, non potest esse Ens reale, nec actu, nec poten- tia, quia ita non haberet definitionem Entis rationis objectivi tantùm, quæ est, ut tantùm esse habeat per intellectum, & extra intellectum sit purum nihil. Quicquid ergo extra intellectum non est purum nihil, seu non involvit contra- dictionem illud Ens reale, si non simpliciter semper & absolutè, saltem diminu- tè, & secundùm quid, ut patet ex superioribus. Cùm igitur Ens rationis objecti- vum tantùm, debeat nec esse, nec posse esse extra intellectum, seu independenter ab operatione intellectus, utique intellectus objectum, seu tale Ens rationis, de- bet esse unum Ens conceptum, tanquam aliud Ens, vel non Ens, tanquam Ens, vel impossibile, ad modum possibilis.
units.tr: If there were a being of reason that was merely objective, then it would be conceived either as a non-being taken as a being, or one being taken as another being, or an impossible thing in the manner of a possible thing. But a non-being cannot be conceived as a being, nor one being as another being, nor an impossible thing as a possible thing. Therefore there is no being of reason that is merely objective. The consequence holds because a being of reason that is merely objective, that is, an object of the intellect, cannot be a real being, either actually or potentially, for then it would not have the definition of a being of reason that is merely objective, which is that it has being only through the intellect and outside the intellect is pure nothing. Whatever is outside the intellect and is not pure nothing, that is, does not involve a contradiction, is a real being, if not simply and absolutely always, at least in a diminished way and in some respect, as is clear from what was said above. Since, then, a being of reason that is merely objective must neither be nor be able to be outside the intellect, that is, independently of the operation of the intellect, the object of the intellect, or such a being of reason, must necessarily be either one being conceived as another being, or a non-being as a being, or an impossible thing in the manner of a possible thing.

units.la: Minor probatur: A. Non potest concipi non Ens, tanquam Ens; I. Ita apprehenderetur in intellectu aliquid esse Ens, & non esse Ens; at apprehendi non potest, quia est simpliciter impossibile, cùm idem non possit simul esse & non esse, sine contradictione: v.gr. Si privationes, puta tenebræ, apprehende- rentur tanquâ entia, apprehenderetur aliquid esse Ens, & esse nō Ens; Non-Ens quidem, cùm privatio sit non-Ens; Ens verò, quia privatio apprehenderetur ut Ens. Quòd si in conceptu privationis tanq. Ens, dicatur concipi tantùm Ens, non autem non-Ens, clarum est, non concipi privationem planè, quia illa est nō-Ens, atque adeò non concipitur non Ens tanquam Ens; quotes enim aliquid apprehenditur, quod non designabatur apprehendendum, non apprehenditur illud, quod designabatur apprehendendum, sed apprehenditur aliquid aliud, id- que in positivis entibus, multò magis in negativis, & privativis. II. Non-Ens planè non potest concipi, ergo non potest concipi ut Ens, quia quod concipi- tur habet sui speciem in intellectu, siquidem concipere est formare alicujus rei speciem in intellectu, sed non Ens seu nihil non potest habere sui speciem in in- tellectu. E. &c.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved thus. A. A non-being cannot be conceived as a being. I. In that case something would be apprehended in the intellect as both a being and a non-being; but this cannot be apprehended, because it is simply impossible, since the same thing cannot be at once a being and a non-being without contradiction. For example, if privations, such as darkness, were apprehended as beings, something would be apprehended as both a being and a non-being: a non-being indeed, since a privation is a non-being, but a being, because the privation would be apprehended as a being. But if it is said that in the concept of a privation as a being, only the being is conceived and not the non-being, it is clear that the privation is not conceived at all, since it is a non-being, and therefore a non-being is not conceived as a being. For whenever something is apprehended that was not designated to be apprehended, the thing that was designated is not apprehended, but something else is; and this holds for positive beings, and much more for negative and privative ones. II. A non-being cannot be conceived at all, and therefore it cannot be conceived as a being, because what is conceived has its species in the intellect; for to conceive is to form the species of some thing in the intellect, but a non-being, or nothing, cannot have its species in the intellect. Therefore, etc.

units.la: B. Non potest concipi unum Ens tanquam aliud Ens; Sicenim non con- ciperetur res concipienda, sed aliquid aliud: e.g. Si quis velit apprehendere ho- minem, & apprehenderet asinum, ille nullo modo hominem, sed asinum concī- peret & apprehenderet, atque adeò non conciperet hominem tanquam asinum, cùm nullo modo apprehendat hominem, sed asinum.
units.tr: B. One being cannot be conceived as another being. For in that case the thing to be conceived would not be conceived, but something else. For example, if someone wished to apprehend a man and apprehended an ass, he would in no way conceive or apprehend a man, but an ass; and so he would not conceive a man as an ass, since he would in no way apprehend a man, but an ass.

units.la: C. Non potest concipi impossibile ad modum possibilis; Impossibile scil. Logicè, quod consistit in repugnantia terminorum: tale nempe quia est purum nihil, non est verum, & quia non est verum, non est intelligibile, quia non est in- telligibile, non potest concipi, quia non potest concipi, non potest esse Ens ra- tionis. Non potest autem concipi, quia in intellectu involveret contradictio- nem: at quod involvit contradictionem, esse dicit non esse, cùm unum destruat essentiam alterius. Ergo Intellectus meus non potest concipere, seu formare ideam equi rationalis, ob repugnantiam terminorum, eo quod rationale destruat essentiam equi, & equus dicat irrationale, consequenter si posset concipere equum rationalem, irrationale conciperem rationale, & equum conciperem non equum, quod impossibile.
units.tr: C. An impossible thing cannot be conceived in the manner of a possible thing. I mean impossible in the logical sense, which consists in the incompatibility of terms. Such a thing, because it is pure nothing, is not true; and because it is not true, it is not intelligible; and because it is not intelligible, it cannot be conceived; and because it cannot be conceived, it cannot be a being of reason. But it cannot be conceived because it would involve a contradiction in the intellect; and what involves a contradiction says that a thing is not what it is, since one term destroys the essence of the other. Therefore my intellect cannot conceive or form the idea of a rational horse, on account of the incompatibility of the terms, since the rational destroys the essence of the horse, and "horse" signifies the irrational. Consequently, if I could conceive a rational horse, I would conceive the irrational as rational, and a horse as not a horse, which is impossible.

units.la: Summa; Aut concipitur possibile, aut impossibile. Si possibile, tum res concepta, non est Ens rationis objectivum tantum, quia independens est ab operatione intellectus, ut supra, & extra intellectum non est purum nihil, impossibile etiam non potest concipi, quia est purum nihil: At puri nihili idea in intellectu non datur; Ergo non potest concipi, & per consequens non potest esse Ens rationis.
units.tr: In summary: either the thing conceived is possible, or it is impossible. If it is possible, then the thing conceived is not a being of reason that is merely objective, because it is independent of the operation of the intellect, as above, and outside the intellect it is not pure nothing. An impossible thing also cannot be conceived, because it is pure nothing; but no idea of pure nothing is given in the intellect. Therefore it cannot be conceived, and consequently it cannot be a being of reason.

units.la: Ex his patet, quid de Monte Aureo sentiendum, cum nempe is extra intellectum, non dicat purum nihil, seu non implicet contradictionem, utique possibile Logicum est; quod habere esse reale diminutum saltem & secundum quid, quo tamen ab Ente rationis objectivo tantum contradistingui possit, ex superioribus dicto VIII no est obscurum. Coronidem praestet illud Plautinum: quod satis est, satis est.
units.tr: From these points it is clear what is to be thought of the Monte Aureo: namely, since it is outside the intellect and does not signify pure nothing, that is, does not involve a contradiction, it is certainly a logical possible, which has real being in a diminished way, at least, and in some respect; and this can be distinguished from a being of reason that is merely objective, as is not obscure from what was said in the eighth point above. Let that Plautine saying serve as the crown: "What is enough is enough."

units.la: In medium ponant qui meliora tenent!
units.tr: Let those who hold the better views put them forward!

units.tr: We assert that the origin of springs lies not in rains or in the air, but in the sea.

units.la: Mas & foemina non differunt specie, proinde qui mulieres homines esse negant, homines sunt non homines.
units.tr: Male and female do not differ in species; therefore those who deny that women are human beings are men who are not men.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Una numero vox ne a duobus quidem audiri potest, nec abunius utraque aure.
units.tr: A single voice, one in number, cannot be heard even by two people, nor by one man with both ears.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Is vere est Philosophus, non qui Aristotelis, vel cujusvis alium mentem, sed qui ipsas rerum naturas & essentias cognoscendo penetrat.
units.tr: He is truly a philosopher who follows not the mind of Aristotle or of anyone else, but who penetrates the very natures and essences of things by knowing them.

units.la: Μόνῳ τῷ Θεῷ δόξα.
units.tr: To God alone be the glory [Μόνῳ τῷ Θεῷ δόξα].

units.la: I. Acclamatio Amicorum:
units.tr: I. Acclamation of Friends:

units.la: Genio & Ingenio florentissimo juveni Viro
units.tr: To the young man of genius and most flourishing talent

units.la: Dn. CASPARO WYSSIO, Assertori Disputationis solertissimo, magno Amore concepta, & harmonica voce emissa.
units.tr: To Dn. CASPAR WYSS, most skilful defender of Disputation, conceived with great affection and sent forth in harmonious voice.

units.la: FAta Deusque sinunt: paullo majora canamus: Heic juvat alternis concinuisse Choris. Wyssius ille placet juvenes cantate Poetæ, Natus Castalidum, candidus ingenio. Plaudite Vos omnes: nam tanta scientia WysI Dignior est omni Carmine, Voce, Stylo. Hæc cecinisse, sat est: Mihi Wysius ille placebit; Incipiant alii: Pausa silere monet.
units.tr: The Fates and God allow it: let us sing of somewhat greater things. Here it pleases us to sing in alternating choirs. That famous Wyss pleases; sing, young poets, born of the Castalian Muses, bright in genius. Applaud, all of you; for Wyss is worthier than any song, voice, or style, by reason of so great learning. It is enough to have sung these things: that famous Wyss will please me. Let others begin; the pause bids silence.

units.la: Affinitatis ergo ita plauditJOHANNES PÆSIUS, V.D.M & Cantor ordinarius.
units.tr: In token of affinity, therefore, thus applauds JOHANN PÆSIUS, V.D.M. and ordinary cantor.

units.la: II. CASPARUS WYSSIUS
units.tr: II. CASPAR WYSS

units.la: Ἀναγραμματιζόμενον. Sic is uva pura Suis.
units.tr: Anagram [Ἀναγραμματιζόμενον]. Thus he is the pure grape of the Swiss.

units.la: CUm generosa suo pubescit Vinea fœtu, Purpurea; curvo Saturni dente resecta; Dant uva Nectar Cultori dulce Lyæi. Tu quia Pierÿ comples carchesia Phœbi Nectare Doctrina, Musarum nobilis Uva, Talia verba refert de Te Φιλόμυσος Achates: Sic Is pura Suis uva est, sic Succus amatus, Sic Tiguro decori magno, ut sunt vitibus Uvæ.
units.tr: When the noble vine swells with its generous fruit, purple, cut by Saturn's curved tooth, its grapes give the cultivator the sweet nectar of Lyaeus. You, because you fill the cups of Phoebus with the nectar of Pierian learning, are the noble grape of the Muses. So Achates, the lover of the Muses [Φιλόμυσος], speaks of you in these words: "Thus he is the pure grape of the Swiss, thus the beloved juice, thus a great ornament to Zurich, as grapes are to the vine."

units.la: Is suavis cursu apis.
units.tr: He is a sweet bee in his course.

units.la: PRata, Semiramios hortos, sylvásque peragrat Et cursu celeri, & murmure suavis apis, Purpureúmque metit Narcissum, Lilia lambit, Et Violas libat, gustat opésque Rosa: Indéque pergrato distendit Nectare cellas, Cultorísque suo dulcia mella parat. Suavis apis cursu est, volitans per amœna Roseta, Gratior & multò Cecropiis apibus, Qui per Natura flores volat altus eburnos, Qui miranda Soli conspicit atque Poli, Notitiaq; favos constipat Nectare dulci, Artibus Aonijs ora referta ferens. Sic legis, en VVyssi, Nectar de vertice Cirrha, Vincis & Hyblaas sedulitate Tua: Hinc de Te merito mittunt hanc pectore vocem, Qui Tua, qua fundis, Thespia mella vident:
units.tr: The bee roams through meadows, the gardens of Semiramis, and the woods, sweet in her swift course and her murmur. She gathers the purple narcissus, licks the lilies, sips the violets, and tastes the riches of the rose. Then she fills her cells with pleasing nectar and prepares sweet honey for her cultivator. He is a sweet bee in his course, flying over pleasant rose beds, and far more pleasing than the Cecropian bees. He flies high over the ivory flowers of nature and looks upon the wonders of the sun and sky, and he packs his honeycombs with sweet nectar of knowledge, bringing back the Aonian arts in his mouth. So you read, behold, Wyss, nectar from the summit of the Muses' spring. You surpass even the Hyblaean bees in your diligence. Hence, rightly, those who see the Thespian honey you pour out send this voice from their hearts about you.

units.la: Suavis apis cursu Is, nam currit ut optima fingat Doctrina mella, & compleat Arte favos. Perge ita: sic clarus rutilis evadere squamis Mox poteris, gravidas ut Maro laudat apes.
units.tr: He is a sweet bee in his course, for he runs so that teaching may shape the finest honey, and fills the combs with skill. Go on in this way: soon you will be able to shine with gleaming scales, as Maro praises the bees laden with honey.

units.la: εἰς φιλίας πεχμήςλον P.Joh. Conradus Heideggerus,S. Theolog. Cand.
units.tr: As a token of friendship [εἰς φιλίας τεκμήριον]. P. Joh. Conradus Heideggerus, candidate of sacred theology.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: MARS PHILOSOPHICUS.
units.tr: PHILOSOPHICAL MARS.

units.la: Terras jam dudum ferro populatur & igniBellipotens Mavors, cristata cassride cinctus;Quaque patet tellus vitreo circumsona PontoClassica saeva tonant, Taratantara dira cientur,Horridus exigitur per viscera saucia mucro,Luctus ubique, nigrae & quam plurima mortis imago est.Gradivus tremulum vaecors sic concutit orbem.Haud multum pugna est Bellonā mitior istā,Ad quam conclamat lituisque tubāque crepanteEffrons turba Sophūm, cui mens & cornea fibra est,Haud equidem heic fuso pinguescunt sanguine campi;Haud Martis pulli portant in bella bipennes,Loricam haud miles ventri succingit atrocem,Haudque Thraso creperus sua spicula lucida tergitArvinā pingui, nec manant stagna cruore.Alter in alterius sed rumpit nomen habenisLaxatis mordax, non hospes ab hospite tutus.Figere discipulus Doctori tentat ocellum,Et placita inflectit tyro veneranda Magistri.Indus, Arabs, Syrus, ac Theuton, recutitus apellaHoc pallent morbo, hac sudant praecordia culpā.
units.tr: Mars, the war-powerful god in his crested helmet, has long been ravaging the lands with sword and fire. Wherever the earth stretches along the glassy sea, trumpets blare and dreadful war-cries are raised, and the savage blade is driven horribly through wounded bowels. Grief is everywhere, and there is hardly a sight that is not an image of black death. Gradivus, frenzied, shakes the trembling world in this way. Battle is scarcely milder than that of Bellona, and to it, with trumpet and bellowing horn, the shameless crowd of the wise calls out, men whose minds are of horn and whose fibre is hard. Certainly the fields here are not fattened with spilled blood. The sons of Mars do not carry axes into battle, a soldier does not gird on a fearsome breastplate over his belly, and the boastful Thraso does not polish his bright darts with greasy fat, nor do pools flow with gore. But the biting man, his reins loosened, breaks the name of another, and no guest is safe from his guest. The pupil tries to pierce the eye of his teacher, and the novice bends the revered opinions of his master. The Indian, the Arab, the Syrian and the German, circumcised or not, turn pale with this disease and sweat in their hearts with this fault.

units.la: Ambigůus Mars est, nec fas heic dicere verum, Sed multò præstant ægri figmenta cerebri, Queis Troili vires audax supplantat Achilles. Pauper Aristoteles olim Phaetontis ad instar Ad Solem evectus, solio decussus ab alto Cogitur ire pedes, verbenas porgere mystis; Hunc rodunt mures, milvi corvique voraces Huic aquilæ obclangunt, odio instigante scelesto; Exhaustus vigor est, macro non corpore succus Ullus inest, miser est, cutis ac vix ossibus hæret. Dogmata sana simul somno moriuntur obeso. Et puer heic nasum vult Rhinocerotis habere, Qui jacet in cunis, nec demorsos sapit ungues. Heic audeto aliquid gyaris & carcere dignum, Si vis esse aliquis, probitas frigescit & alget, Criminibus debent hortos, prætoria, mensas, Argentum vetus, & stantem extra pocula caprum. Dixeris Harpyias Sophiæ mala cuncta dedisse, Inque omnes orci prolem se didere terras. Sed pereat, cuicunque placet phanaticus error, Palleat, ut nudis pressit qui calcibus anguem; Prælia dira Sophûm vadant Acherontis ad umbras, Ambitio cineres Cocyti quæsitet imi. Constet honos Sophiæ, mitis concordia regnet! Sed mihi cur tantâ siccum jecur ardeat irâ, Inquiras, Wyssi, juvenum flos, laudis Ephœbe? Devia consector, Satyri en latitare sub umbra Conor & umbone hoc, quia non mihi lactea vena Sustinet in laudes manare tuas, nec Apollo Consultus mihi plectra dedit, conatibus impar Musa tuis hæc est, tanta sub mole fatiscit. Macte gravi studio, macte immortalibus orsis
units.tr: Mars is ambiguous, and it is not right to say the truth here, but the fictions of a sick brain far surpass it, by which bold Achilles overthrows the strength of Troilus. Poor Aristotle, once raised to the sun like Phaethon, thrown down from his high throne, is forced to go on foot and offer verbena to the initiates. Mice gnaw at him, and greedy kites and crows; eagles scream at him, with wicked hatred stirring them on. His vigour is exhausted, there is no juice left in his thin body, he is wretched, his skin barely clings to his bones. Sound doctrines die together with the obese sleep. And here a boy wants to have the nose of a rhinoceros, though he lies in his cradle and does not yet know how to bite his nails. Here, if you wish to be someone, dare to do something worthy of the stocks and prison. Integrity grows cold and shivers; they owe their gardens, their praetorian palaces, their tables, old silver, and the goat that stands outside the cups to their crimes. You would say the Harpies have given all evils to Wisdom and scattered their offspring across all the lands of the underworld. But let whatever fanatical error pleases anyone perish, let him turn pale, as one who pressed a snake with bare heels. Let the dire battles of the wise go down to the shadows of Acheron; let ambition seek the ashes of deepest Cocytus. Let the honour of Wisdom stand, let mild concord reign! But why, you ask, Wyssius, flower of the young, Ephebus of praise, does my liver burn dry with such great anger? I pursue the byways and try to hide under the shade of a satyr, and I do this with a shield, because my milky vein cannot pour forth in praise of you, and Apollo, when consulted, has not given me the plectrum. The Muse is unequal to your efforts; she sinks under so great a weight. Hail to you for your serious study, hail to your undying undertakings.

units.la: HUIUS CUS VYSSIUS S.T. Doct. Sind
units.tr: TO THIS SAME VYSSIUS, Doctor of Sacred Theology, of Sind.

units.la: Ingenii, rarâ quod finxit ab arte Prometheus.Te Pater Æneas, te patruus excitat HectorQui Patriæ nati, qui nil nisi celsa volutant.Olim ubi te matura viris transcripserit ætas,Sisyphia arx fuerit quando expugnata laborum;Nî vatem auguriis fallacibus implet Apollo;Præmia captabis, non ære incisa notisque,Qualia tempus edax lento consumere tractuSæpe solet, sed quæ vires acquirit ab ævo,Amplior ac duro te fama beabit Ulysse.
units.tr: Of the genius which Prometheus fashioned by rare art. Your father Aeneas and your uncle Hector rouse you, who were born for the fatherland and who think only of lofty things. Once your ripe age has enrolled you among men, the Sisyphean citadel will be taken when its labours are over, unless Apollo, with deceptive auguries, fills you as a poet. You will win prizes not carved in bronze and marks, such as devouring time is often wont to wear away with slow erosion, but such as acquire strength from the age, and fame, greater and more lasting, will make you blessed, as it did Ulysses.

units.la: Hisce animi sui candorem & officia quæque oppigneratJoh. Henricus Heideggerus,S.S.Theol.Stud.Tigur.
units.tr: In pledge of the candour of his mind and of every duty to this man, Joh. Henricus Heideggerus, S.S. Theol. Stud., Tigur.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Epigramma.
units.tr: Epigram.

units.la: Nil scit, scire putans se: non, mihi scire videtur.
units.tr: He knows nothing while thinking he knows; to me he does not seem to know.

units.la: Scit {bene, male} qui sentit, se {bene male} scire nihil.
units.tr: He knows, well or badly, who feels that he knows nothing, well or badly.

units.la: Vera / Falsa latent, & {falsa vera} patent: hæc omnia doctus
units.tr: True things lie hidden and false things lie open; learned man, you will know all these things.

units.la: Illis {non quæstis, haud neglectis, per-} bene doctus eris.
units.tr: With these things neither sought nor neglected, you will be very well taught.

units.la: Posuit IOH. RODOLPHUS VVYSSIUS, Theol. Stud.
units.tr: Set down by Joh. Rudolphus Wyssius, student of theology.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Nil mihi cum Phœbo, nil cum permeside lympha,Nec lauro placuit composuisse comas.Est labor iste meus, modulanti dicit Apollo:Hoc solùm cœptis, GRATULOR, addo tuis.
units.tr: I have nothing to do with Phoebus, nothing with the water of Permessus, and I did not care to arrange my hair with laurel. This labour is mine, and Apollo says to me as I tune my lyre: "To your undertakings I add only this: I CONGRATULATE you."

units.la: Συγγενείας ἀμβολον ponit HULDRICUS VVYSSIUS, S.Theol.Stud.
units.tr: Places the token of kinship [Συγγενείας ἀμβολον]: HULDRICUS VVYSSIUS, S.Theol.Stud.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Epigramma Jambico-reciprocum.
units.tr: A Jambic Reciprocal Epigram.

units.la: Micent nitore tecta sublimi aurea, Domus labore structa Carum & splendeat: Magis quieta bella, Musae heroides Nitent, amore quovis humano acrius. Struit amore junctus almo has Wyssius Theses; canora Musa sertum at construet, Dabit Minerva prima laudem Aonidum Tibi, diserta turba, Musarum optima. Viam juvante vade Clio hanc sapius, Scies suprema quaque doctrina omnia.
units.tr: Golden roofs gleam with lofty brilliance, a house built with the labour of Carus and made to shine. More quiet wars, heroic Muses, shine more keenly than any human love. Wyssius, joined to these by gentle love, builds these Theses; the tuneful Muse will also weave a garland. Minerva will give you, the first of the Aonian Muses, eloquent throng, best of the Muses, the first praise. Go on your way with Clio's help and read this often, and you will know all the highest learning.

units.la: In perpetuum ἀνεπικτήτῳ Φιλίας μνημόσυνον scripsit HENRICUS WYSSIUS, Tigurinus.
units.tr: In perpetuity, an unpurchasable memorial of friendship [ἀνεπικτήτῳ Φιλίας μνημόσυνον], written by Henricus Wyssius, of Zurich.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Gloria magna sat est, & opis non indiga nostrae, Ipsum laudat opus quemlibet artificem. Dignus es, ô Wysi, caput Attica nectat oliva, Cervicémque tegat digna corolla tuam. Hic fructus studii, vigilatorúmque laborum, Praeditus hic quo sis munere nempe patet. Ipse Deus faveat facilis sublimibus ausis, Dignáque pro meritis praemia ferre sinat.
units.tr: Great glory is enough and needs no help from ours; the work itself praises any craftsman. You are worthy, O Wyss: let the Attic olive bind your head, and let a fitting garland cover your neck. This is the fruit of your study and watchful labours, and by this gift it is plainly seen what you are endowed with. May God himself favour your bold undertakings with ease, and allow you to bear rewards worthy of your merits.

units.la: Amicitia nunquam intermoritura Symbolon SOLOMONIS PEIERI, Philosophiae Studiosi, Helvetio-Schaphusiani.
units.tr: Amicitia nunquam intermoritura Symbolon of SOLOMON PEIER, student of philosophy, of Schaffhausen in Switzerland.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: NEc Musa possēt dicere: beatè Vena fluxit. Quid ergo? Rorat carmina in Corde, non in venis. Deabus ille VVTSSIUS vel Phœbus est, vel fallit. Probatur forma Corporis, et Mentis, his Deabus. Sed prodit his Amoribus, quod nos latere nolunt. Itáne, FLOS amabilis, DEAS amare nôsti? Id jure juro: Vatibus hic ardor est canendus. Canemus: Vivat VVTSSIUS, et turba dicat: AMEN.
units.tr: Nor could the Muse say: the vein flowed happily. What then? It drips songs from the heart, not from the veins. That VVTSSIUS is either a goddess or Phoebus, or else he deceives. Beauty of body and of mind is proved by these goddesses. But by these loves he reveals what they are unwilling to keep hidden. Are you so, lovable FLOS, that you know how to love goddesses? I swear it with good reason: this ardour is what poets must sing. Let us sing: Long live VVTSSIUS, and let the crowd say: Amen.
